activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
The sign-in table at the food bank smelled of wet cardboard and green bananas, and Aiden wrote his name in a binder already soft from hundreds of other signatures. He had come because his mother had mentioned it once, lightly, over dinner in October, and because the college application essay he had half drafted needed something behind it besides grades. Mr. Navarro, who taught civics and organized the Saturday crews, handed him a paper wristband and pointed toward a group of teenagers loading crates into a van. "You're on the glean," he said. Aiden did not ask what that meant. He was tired of asking things.

Kacey was already in the van, boots up on a cooler, and beside her sat Lisa, who had been in his chemistry class and had never once spoken to him. Kacey spoke immediately, as if they had been mid conversation for years. "You're the last one. If we're late the farmer starts without us and then we get the squash nobody else wanted, which is, like, doubly unwanted squash." Lisa smiled at the window. Aiden climbed in over her knees and sat where he could see the road.

The field was twenty minutes out, past a strip mall and a church with a leaning steeple. The farmer met them at the gate with a thermos and the unhurried manner of a man who had already been working for three hours. The main harvest had gone out on trucks that week, Kacey explained as they walked the rows, and what remained was theirs. Aiden looked down the furrows and saw them strewn with squash, crooked ones, small ones, ones hidden under leaves the pickers had missed. He had assumed a harvested field would be empty.

"So all this would just rot," he said.

"Unless we come get it," Lisa said. She crouched and lifted a butternut the size of a forearm out of the mud. "That's the whole thing. Gleaning, it's called. Volunteers pick what's left in the field after the main harvest so it doesn't go to waste." She set it in her crate with a small knock, like a full stop.

They worked the morning in a line. Aiden found a rhythm quickly, the bend and lift and stack of it, and his mind drifted in the way it did during long runs. He had come, he admitted to himself, partly to have something presentable to say about himself, to aggrandize a Saturday into a character. But the squash did not care about his essay. It was simply there, in the mud, in quantities that made his idea of generosity seem parsimonious, a few coins in a jar compared with rows and rows of food that existed only because nobody had bothered to want it. He thought about his draft, the phrase about giving back, and felt the slight shame of having written sentences that sounded better than they were.

At the far end of the field the ground dipped and the rows became a morass of standing water and crushed leaves, and Kacey lost a boot in it to the ankle, laughing, hauling herself out with one hand on Aiden's shoulder. Lisa stood on the higher ground passing crates across the gap, her sleeves rolled, calling out numbers. Three hundred and six, three hundred and twelve. The farmer watched from the gate with his thermos and said nothing, which Aiden decided was his version of approval.

On the drive back, the crates shifting behind them at every turn, Kacey asked what he would write about it. "The essay," she said. "You're doing this for an essay, right? Everyone here is doing this for an essay." Lisa looked at him with what might have been sympathy or might have been a test.

"I don't know yet," Aiden said. He watched the fields go past, already half emptied of what they had held. "Maybe that I showed up for one reason and I'm leaving with about four, and I can't rank them yet." Kacey considered this, then turned up the radio. Lisa leaned forward between the seats and said, "Three hundred and twelve," one more time, to no one in particular, and put a squash-marked hand on his shoulder to steady herself as the van took the corner.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in his 1863 book on drama technique.
story:
Nobody at the Millbrook Community Theatre cared about the ten-minute play festival, and I include myself in that, which is why it was so annoying that I couldn't stop thinking about mine. Mr. Kowalski had posted the assignment on the corkboard by the concession stand: each of us would write and stage a short play drawn from a moment in our own lives. Rehearsals began in two weeks. I told Hector I'd probably write about the time I got locked in the library overnight, which was a lie, because I had already decided, in secret, to write about the winter my father lost his job and I sold my trumpet to pay for the heating bill. That had actually happened, more or less. Some of the details were negotiable.

The theatre smelled like dust and burnt coffee, and the radiator worked on a schedule known only to itself, so we rehearsed in coats. Aikam was directing my piece because she claimed she had "an eye," and because she had bartered her services for my help painting flats for her one-woman show about the French Revolution, which she described, without apparent irony, as a plutocracy takedown. "The rich run everything, Simon," she said, jabbing a brush at me. "Even here. Who do you think paid for this building? Not the audience." I said the audience paid for tickets, and she said that proved my innocence, and we left it there.

The trouble was the shape of the thing. My script began with the trumpet going into the pawnshop window and ended with the heat coming back on, and in between Aikam kept circling it with a red pen like a shark that had read somewhere that circling was intimidating. "It's all one temperature," she said. "It's glacial, and then it's still glacial, and then it's over. Where does it turn?"

I didn't know, and I wasn't going to admit that, so I said the turn was obviously the pawnshop scene, and she said then why was the second half twice as long, and I said artistic balance, and she went to get a napkin from the concession stand without dignifying that.

She came back and drew a triangle on it with a felt pen, splitting it into slices. "Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid," she said, "exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution. Eighteen sixty-three, some book on drama technique. My cousin made me memorize it for auditions." She tapped the napkin. "He died in, like, the eighteen hundreds, so he can't argue with you, but I can. Your exposition is the pawnshop. Your climax is not the pawnshop. The climax is the top of the pyramid. It's the highest point. Where's yours?"

I looked at the triangle. Somewhere under the rising action, in my head, was the night my father found out what I'd done and I said I'd done it for the family, which was maybe half true, and he said he would have rather been cold, which I had been trying very hard for about four months not to think about. "I don't have a climax," I said. "I have an argument we never finished."

"Then write the argument," Aikam said. "That's the whole point of the pyramid, probably. The shape wants you to climb."

Hector, who had wandered over to steal popcorn, read the napkin upside down and announced that his play, a comedy about a bank robbery conducted entirely by mime, was one hundred percent climax from the first line. "Falling action is for cowards," he said. Aikam told him his play would collapse like a tent, and he said at least it would collapse quickly, which in his mouth was nearly a compliment to my slower disaster.

I went home and rewrote the second half so that the unfinished argument sat at the peak, and the falling action was my father standing at the window with the pawnshop ticket in his hand, not going, and the resolution was just the two of us eating soup while the radiator ticked. In rehearsal the argument scene worked, mostly. Hector played my father, which was absurd, since Hector is sixteen and laughs at his own shoes, but he went quiet in a way I hadn't known he could, and the line about rather being cold landed in the dark of the empty house like a coin dropped down a stairwell.

Opening night, my father came. I had told him the play was about something else, which was a lie of the usual kind, and afterward he found me by the concession stand holding a napkin with a triangle drawn on it, because I had never thrown it away. He looked at the pyramid for a long moment, then at me, and said, "You sold the trumpet in March. The heat didn't go off until February."

"Artistic balance," I said.

He turned the napkin right side up.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
story:
The lawn chair had a broken strap, so Makayla sat with her notebook balanced on her knees, the biology textbook open on the patio table where the wind kept lifting its pages. Her mother had said to work inside, but the kitchen smelled like onions and the backyard felt like the only place where Saturday afternoon would leave her alone. On the page in front of her was a strand of DNA, a string of letters the textbook wanted her to copy into RNA and then decode into a protein, and below it, in her handwriting, was an answer that the answer key in the back refused to agree with.

She had done it the way she thought she was supposed to. Wherever the DNA had an A, she wrote a T, because that was the pairing she remembered, A with T and G with C, drilled into her since freshman year. But the key gave a different chain of letters for the RNA, and no amount of squinting at her work showed her where she had gone wrong. She checked the DNA letters one at a time, mouthing them, tapping the pencil against each base like she was counting change that kept coming up short.

Kiera let herself in through the side gate, which she had been doing since they were nine, and dropped onto the other chair with her phone in her hand. She was going to a show tonight at the community center, some band whose drummer she had a crush on, and she wanted Makayla there by eight, and she had been making this case since Tuesday with the persistence of a debt collector.

"I can't," Makayla said, not looking up. "I failed the last quiz. Ms. Banerjee gave me a retake Monday morning, before school, and if I fail it again I'm done for the quarter."

"You pontificate about how you never do anything fun, and then when fun shows up at your gate, you're out here romancing a textbook." Kiera stretched her legs onto the table, nearly landing her sneaker on the open page.

"It's not the textbook, it's the key. It's wrong, or I'm wrong, and I can't tell which, and it's driving me insane."

Kiera leaned over, actually looked, and Makayla felt a small flare of hope. But Kiera was in a different class, with a teacher who let things slide, and she just said, "Looks like letters to me," and went back to her phone.

The wind turned another page, and Makayla flattened it with her palm and started over from the beginning, slower this time, the way Ms. Banerjee had once told them to do with anything that mattered: read the question before you trust your answer. The DNA read A, T, G, C, in some order. Where the DNA said A, she had written T in her RNA. Where the key said the RNA should say something else. She laid her answer beside the key, letter by letter, and stopped on the first A in the DNA strand. She had put a T. The key had put a U.

She sat very still. Somewhere at the edge of the yard a sprinkler ticked on, and the water hissed against the fence, and she held the pencil without moving it. T versus U. In every row, the same substitution, exactly where she had matched adenine with thymine. And the sentence from some half-remembered class came back to her, not in Ms. Banerjee's voice but in the flat voice of the textbook itself: in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine. Not only in DNA did A pair with T and G pair with C; in RNA the rule changed, and she had carried the old rule across the border like contraband. She flipped back to the chapter and found it in the third paragraph, and there it was, plain as a stop sign, and she had read it on Tuesday and it had gone in one ear and out the other.

"It's U," she said out loud.

"It's you what?" Kiera said.

"Uracil. In RNA it's U, not T. I've been writing T the whole time. Every single answer." She laughed once, a strange short sound, half relief and half disgust at herself. She erased her chain of letters and copied it again, U where the U belonged, and when she decoded it into the protein the key finally matched, amino acid for amino acid, no argument left.

Cooper texted a few minutes later asking about the show, and Kiera typed back without asking Makayla first. Makayla watched her do it, then looked down at the corrected page. The DNA had done its work quietly, the way it always did, and she had spent three hours fighting a rule she thought she already knew instead of checking whether the rule still applied. She was aware, in some corner of her mind, that this was almost tautological, that she had been wrong because she had assumed she was right, and that the retake on Monday would ask her to know things she hadn't yet discovered she was missing.

"Tell Cooper maybe," she said. "If I get through the last two problems. And Kiera, if I start explaining DNA at the show, just take my drink away."

Kiera grinned and held up the phone. "Say the thing again. Uracil."

"Uracil," Makayla said, and wrote it, and the sprinkler hissed against the fence in the dark coming on.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
story:
The rain had stopped by the time Simon unzipped the tent, but the fly still held water, and it extruded a thin cold ribbon down his sleeve when he pushed past it. He carried the laptop like something wounded, both hands, elbows in, and set it on the picnic table under the tarp where the others were boiling water for instant oatmeal. Ms. Robinson looked over from the stove. "You brought that thing to the woods," she said. It was not quite a question. "I brought the woods to that thing," Simon said, and opened it, angling the screen away from the glare.

He was making a map for a scholarship application, due in nine days. The idea had seemed simple in his bedroom: take the city's flood risk layer, lay it over the housing layer, and show which neighborhoods sat inside the hundred-year floodplain. His father, who built storm drains for the county, had described the idea over dinner with an enthusiasm he rarely spent on anything except concrete. "Nobody argues with a map," he'd said. Simon had liked that. It sounded like proof.

Josef came back from the creek with wet boots and no fish and leaned over Simon's shoulder. The two layers were on screen together now, the floodplain a pale green wash, the housing parcels a lattice of thin gray lines. "Which one's the river?" Josef asked. "The blue squiggle," Simon said. Josef pointed at the blue squiggle, which ran directly through the middle of City Hall, bisected the courthouse, and clipped a corner of the middle school. "That's the river," Simon said again, more quietly, because it wasn't.

He checked the parcels against his memory of the actual city, the one he'd driven through for seventeen years. The blocks were all there, the right shapes, the right names in the right order, but displaced, everything sitting a few hundred meters from where it belonged. The flood layer, meanwhile, was exactly right; he could see the oxbow near Lauryn's street, the low sweep of parkland by the bridge. Two truthful maps, apparently, superimposed into one lie.

"Maybe the river moved," Josef offered. "Rivers do that." "Not through City Hall by Thursday." Lauryn arrived with her oatmeal and her hood still up, and watched him toggle the layers off and on, off and on, like a man blinking at an optical illusion. Somewhere in the layer properties he found it: the two files listed different coordinate reference systems, each a string of numbers and abbreviations he didn't recognize, each layer speaking its own private grid. The flood layer had been built in one; the housing layer lived in another. Neither was wrong. They simply did not agree on where anything was.

Lauryn had assumed, when she signed up for the trip, that she would spend it being cold and pretending to enjoy it. Instead she was sitting under a tarp watching Simon mutter at a laptop while Ms. Robinson, ordinarily patient, grew irascible about the stove's refusal to light. Lauryn's father lived in the second ward, the one that flooded, the one Simon's green wash was meant to be about. She had opinions about people making maps of her street from forty miles away. "So fix it," she said. "It's not a broken map," Simon said. "It's two maps that don't line up." "Then fix the lining up."

He found a tool called reproject. He told the housing layer to reproject into the flood layer's coordinate reference system, and the parcels slid across the screen like a scattered deck being gathered up, and then everything clicked into place. The river returned to its channel. City Hall stood on dry land. The green wash settled over the eastern blocks, and Lauryn, watching, put her spoon down. "That's it," she said. "That's my dad's whole street."

They looked at it together for a while. The neighborhoods in the floodplain were not random; Lauryn named them the way you name relatives. Simon understood, then, the thing his father had missed, or maybe had known all along and not said: the map was true now, and truth was not the same as neutrality. He also understood that he couldn't tell from a green wash which houses were rentals, which families could leave for a week and which couldn't, who had flood insurance and who had been told the drainage project would handle it. There was a kind of solipsism in trusting the data too completely, as if the city existed only as it was stored; there was a different kind in trusting only what you'd personally driven past. He wanted both, and he did not yet know how to put both on one map.

"The scholarship people want conclusions," he said. "What are you going to give them?" Lauryn asked. "The map," Simon said. "And a paragraph saying what the map can't tell me." Josef, from the creek bank, called out that he'd finally caught something, and when they went to look it was a stick. Simon left the laptop open under the tarp, the green wash glowing against the gathering dark, the river running where the river ran.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Joseph had never ruined a meal in his life, which was a claim he made often enough that his younger sister had started saying it back to him in a flat voice whenever he entered the kitchen. Tonight he was making dinner for the whole family on his own, chicken breasts with lemon and rice, because his mother had taken the late shift at the hospital and his father was three weeks into the kind of silence that followed arguments nobody would repeat aloud. Joseph had volunteered to cook partly to be useful and partly, though he did not introspect on this too deeply, because a kitchen gave him a reason to stay home on a Friday.

The recipe was simple and he trusted his instincts over the printed page, which had never once misled him. He browned the breasts in the good pan, slid them into the oven, and set about the rice with the confidence of someone who had watched his mother do this a hundred times without ever actually doing it himself. Halfway through he realized he was not certain how long the chicken had been in, or whether the oven had fully preheated, and he decided the timer must be wrong rather than that he had forgotten to press it.

He pulled the pan out at what felt like the right moment. When he cut into the largest breast the flesh near the bone was faintly pink, and the juices sat in the cut without running clear. His first thought was that this was fine. Pink meant juicy. Restaurants served it that way. He was already composing the sentence he would say at the table when a text from Edison lit up his phone: Edison's family had food poisoning last month from a takeout place, all of them sick for two days, and he had become insufferable about it since. Joseph had laughed at him then. He did not laugh now.

He called Mr. Ramírez, whose kitchen window faced theirs across the narrow side yard and who had, over the years, rescued Joseph's family with a ladder, a jumper cable, and occasional opinions about their gutters. Joseph explained the situation in the tone of someone asking a casual, unimportant question. Mr. Ramírez said to hold on, and four minutes later he was at their back door, holding a thin metal probe with a digital readout, still in his slippers.

"You don't guess with chicken," Mr. Ramírez said. "The food safety people say it's done at 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 Celsius, and you measure that with a thermometer, not your eyes." He handed it over and did not come inside, which Joseph understood as a courtesy, an awareness that the house contained an argument still cooling in its walls. Joseph slid the probe into the thickest part of the biggest breast. The number climbed and settled at 151, a full fourteen degrees short, in territory he had been about to serve with lemon slices on top.

It occurred to him, waiting for the oven to reheat, that his certainty had been a kind of story he told about himself, a truism he had repeated until it substituted for evidence. That was a pernicious habit, he thought, not because confidence was bad but because his brand of it made him unable to see the difference between what he knew and what he had merely decided. He texted Edison a photo of the thermometer reading 167, the chicken now safely past the mark, and got back a single thumbs-up, which felt like being forgiven for something he had never actually said out loud.

His mother came home at nine with her coat still on and her eyes doing that tired bright thing they did when she was trying to seem fine. She sat at the table and ate everything, both servings of the chicken he had held back for her and for himself, and she said it was better than the restaurant on Delancey, and he let her say it because arguing with a compliment was a worse crime than accepting one. He did not tell her about the thermometer, or the pink, or the fourteen degrees. Some honesty you practiced in private first.

Later, wrapping the leftovers, he found himself thinking about his father, who was also somewhere being certain, presumably, about whatever the argument had been about. Joseph understood that he was doing that thing where a small lesson about chicken pretended to be a large lesson about everything, and he stopped himself, because that was its own kind of dishonesty. The chicken was safe. That was all he actually knew. The probe went back across the yard, and Mr. Ramírez answered his door holding a half-eaten sandwich.

"You'll want one of these for yourself," Mr. Ramírez said. "Ten dollars at any hardware store."

"I'll borrow yours again," Joseph said, and Mr. Ramírez closed the door before Joseph could tell whether he had smiled.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Dividing a large batch into shallow containers helps it cool quickly in the fridge, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours.
story:
The shopping list had taken Alexa three days, which seemed absurd until she explained it to Scott on the bus. Seven dinners, one pot of soup, one tray of baked chicken, a grain she could not pronounce, and a total budget of twenty-two dollars, achieved through what Scott kept calling soup arbitrage: markdown vegetables at nine at night, dried beans in bulk, the whole ham bone the butcher gave away for free. "It's not arbitrage if you're just poor and organized," Alexa said, but she wrote it at the top of the plan anyway, in the margin, where the plan could afford a joke.

The community kitchen occupied the basement of the library annex, and Mr. Sharma ran it the way some people run governments: quietly, with a clipboard, and with strong opinions nobody dared argue with. He had agreed to let four students use the ovens on Saturdays, provided they planned their week in advance, costed it to the cent, and cleaned the range before they left. Alexa suspected the cleaning clause was the real point of the whole arrangement. Her mother thought the meal planning was the real point, though her mother also called it "home economics," which Alexa had asked her, twice, to stop doing.

Maggie was already there when Alexa arrived, stirring a stockpot the size of a small bathtub. Her grandmother's chicken and rice soup, she said, from the littoral town where her grandmother had grown up, where every recipe started with a whole bird and ended with enough food for a street. It smelled extraordinary. It also, Alexa noticed, filled the pot to within two inches of the rim, and the fridge was small and temperamental and shared by everyone in the program.

"Mr. Sharma says the soup has to be in the fridge by one," Maggie said, lifting the lid, letting out a cloud of steam that fogged the window over the sink. "It's one now and it's still molten."

Alexa checked her notebook, where she had copied, without much thinking, a line from the laminated card taped inside the cupboard: divide a large batch into shallow containers so it cools quickly, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours. At the time she'd assumed it was about spills. Now she stood in front of the open fridge, doing the arithmetic of heat and volume and one o'clock, and understood that she was holding the difference between soup and a science experiment.

They found the shallow containers in the cupboard under the register, the ones with the blue lids, and a soup ladle, and a funnel that turned out to be unnecessary because Maggie had the wrist of someone raised on enormous pots. They decanted the whole batch into eight flat containers, maybe two inches deep each, and lined them on the middle shelf like files. Alexa left the digital thermometer in one, mostly because she wanted to watch the number fall, and partly, she admitted to herself, because she had been the one to read the card and she wanted proof.

The trouble came at two, when Mr. Sharma did his walkthrough. Scott had put his chicken thighs on the top shelf, uncovered, dripping into Alexa's second container of soup, and Mr. Sharma stood over the fridge with his clipboard and asked, in a voice of profound administrative disappointment, whose chicken was bleeding into the soup. Scott pointed at Alexa, which was a betrayal, though a small one, since he had also been the one to suggest moving the soup to make room for his chicken in the first place. Alexa was exonerated by the thermometer, which she retrieved and held up: the soup in the contaminated container read forty degrees, and the soup in the untouched ones read the same, cooled through in under an hour, all of it safe, only one container lost. Mr. Sharma looked at the flat blue row, then at Alexa, and said nothing, which from him was a parade.

The twist, as Alexa thought of it later, was not the chicken. The twist was Sunday, when she came back for her containers and found Mr. Sharma repacking the community kitchen's own leftover curry into the same shallow blue containers, in the same two-inch layers, with the unhurried movements of a man who had done it ten thousand times. He had never mentioned it. He had simply left the card taped inside the cupboard at exactly eye level, which Alexa now understood was not storage but pedagogy, and she still hadn't decided whether that was generous or sneaky or both.

She took her soup home in a canvas bag, four containers, Monday through Thursday, and gave one to Scott as tax for the accusation and the chicken drippings, an arrangement he accepted with the grace of someone who knew he had gotten the better end of the week. What stayed uncertain was Friday, and the Friday after that, and whether planning could survive a month of this, but Thursday night she set a flat container on the counter to thaw, and Maggie texted a photo of her grandmother's town, the harbor low and silver in it, and wrote, "we should do the seafood one next."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
story:
Emily spread the photocopied population pyramid across the kitchen table and weighted its corners with her mother's teacups, a mug of cold coffee, and a bottle of hot sauce. The assignment from Ms. Banerjee was due Monday: choose a country, read its pyramid, and argue whether it would need more primary schools or more nursing homes in thirty years. Emily had chosen Japan because the shape was dramatic, a barrel cinched at the middle, wide at the top, and narrow at the base like a vase holding all its flowers at the crown.

Rita arrived at four with her own pyramid still in her bag, which she had no intention of taking out. She had come, she said, to eat Emily's food and avoid her own house, where her brothers were being monsters, and she dropped onto the chair across from Emily and propped her chin in her hands.

"What's wrong with yours?" Rita asked, pointing at the diagram. "It's crooked."

"That's the thing. It's not crooked." Emily ran her pencil up the bars. "The whole left side is men and the right side is women. And look, at the bottom, under five, it's almost even. Boys, girls, boys, girls. But up here." She tapped the eighty-and-over band. "The right side sticks way out. There's this big wedge of women and hardly any men. I thought Ms. Banerjee photocopied it badly."

Rita leaned over the page, chewing a strand of her hair. She squinted at the numbers printed along the axes, then sat back with the particular confidence of someone about to guess. "It's probably that women live longer than men," she said. "Like, on average. My grandma's still going and my grandpa's been dead nine years. So the top of it would just be more women than men, wouldn't it."

Emily looked at the page again and felt something shift, the way a word you've misread for a whole paragraph suddenly rearranges itself. The lopsided top wasn't an error or a quirk. It was information. She flipped to the front of her textbook and checked three other pyramids: Italy, Germany, Russia. Every one of them widened on the women's side at the top, though some more than others. On the Nigeria pyramid the asymmetry was barely a whisper; on Japan's it was a shout. She copied the observation into her notes in the margin, then underlined it, then felt embarrassed by the underline and turned it into a box.

"So for the nursing homes thing," Rita said, reaching across to steal the hot sauce for no reason, "you're saying the top part is mostly grandmas."

"Basically." Emily was already writing. If the eighty-year-olds were predominantly women, then the future residents of any nursing home this country built would be too. Rooms, staffing, even the way the buildings were designed, all of it would answer to this shape. She thought of her own grandmother, who had moved into a flat near the sea after her husband died and had seemed, in the first year, like someone reprieved from a sentence, taking up bridge and walking the promenade every morning with a fierce, almost frightening appetite. Emily had never asked her whether she missed him. She asked her about the weather instead, every Sunday, and the weather always held.

The competing half of the question was the base of the pyramid, and there Emily's argument stalled. The bottom bars were thin and getting thinner, which pointed toward fewer children, fewer schools, empty classrooms sold off as flats. But Ms. Banerjee had warned them, in that dry way she had, that a pyramid only showed the present arranged by age, that it was a photograph and not a forecast. A government could change immigration policy, or birth rates could drift upward for reasons no diagram contained. Emily had a whole paragraph drafted about the shrinking base before she understood that her certainty was embryonic, an argument with a heartbeat but no bones, and she struck through it and started a different paragraph that began, "If present patterns hold."

Her mother came through the kitchen at six, glanced at the table with its teacup anchors, and asked whether either of them wanted dinner. Rita said yes immediately, being Rita. Emily said she'd eat later, and her mother's hand rested for a moment on the back of her chair, a small pressure that meant nothing and everything, before she went to the stove.

"It's weird," Emily said to Rita, while the pan heated and the kitchen began to smell of onions. "The graph tells you two opposite stories at once. The bottom says build nothing, the top says build everything for old women. And I keep wanting to pick one and be done."

"So pick the grandmas," Rita said. "They vote more anyway." She was joking, but Emily wrote it down, then crossed it out, then wrote it again in the margin where the facts she couldn't yet verify lived, the small electric charges that might, if she tracked them down, ionize the whole argument into something solid. She sat looking at the pyramid until the light through the window went from white to gold and the onions started to hiss.

"Rita, tell me again why the top's like that," she said, pencil ready.

"Women live longer than men, on average. I told you."

Emily wrote it down. Then she turned the page sideways, so the pyramid lay flat like a landscape, wide old ranges on the right and a narrow river delta on the left, and for a long moment she just looked at it, the whole country lying there on her kitchen table, deciding quietly what to build.

"Do you think people can change a shape like that," she asked, "or only react to it?"

Rita stole a piece of raw pepper and said, "I think Ms. Banerjee grades on the thesis statement."

Emily laughed, capped her pen, and set the table.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale lists a change in residence as a stressful life event worth 20 points, the same as a change in schools.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else, and Chase stood in the middle of the living room holding a box marked KITCHEN, MISC, which was a lie, because inside were two sweaters, a dead phone charger, and the frisbee Camilo had signed in silver marker last June. Outside, the moving truck had already gone. His mother was somewhere arguing with a curtain rod. The floors were bare wood, and every footstep he took sounded like it belonged to someone else.

He called Camilo on the second try. "You're in a cave," Camilo said. "You sound like you're in a cave."

"Empty house. It's like a gymnasium in here." Chase sat down on the floor because there was nowhere else to sit, and the frisbee box tipped over beside him. He told Camilo about the twelve-hour drive, about how his father had claimed the first shower in the new bathroom like it was a historical event, about the grocery store where the cashier had asked if they were the new family on Juniper, as if the whole town had been briefed.

"You should've seen your replacement," Camilo said. "We got a kid named Trevor who can't catch." There was a pause with a little laughter in it, and then both of them let the silence stretch, because the joke had done its job and they both knew what came after the job was done.

After they hung up, Chase heard a knock. A man stood in the open doorway holding a covered dish, and behind him, on the sidewalk, a girl about Chase's age was pretending very hard to be interested in a hedge. "Mr. Santos-Reyes," the man said. "From next door. This is Kierra, she lives three doors down and has appointed herself welcome committee, which I did not ask for." Kierra waved with two fingers, still studying the hedge.

They ended up sitting on the living room floor with the dish between them, some kind of pasta Chase ate too much of, and Kierra did most of the talking while he did the nodding. At some point he mentioned, almost apologizing, that he was tired in a way that didn't make sense, since all he'd done for two days was sit in a car and carry boxes lighter than the ones at his old job. "My mom says I'm being dramatic. I mean, I'm seventeen, so, statistically." He expected her to agree with his mother.

"Look it up," Kierra said, already pulling out her phone. "Psychologists actually count this. The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale. It's a checklist of life events with point values." She scrolled, then turned the screen toward him. "A change in residence is on there. Twenty points. Same as a change in schools." She said it the way you'd read off a menu, but Chase took the phone and read it twice, and something in his chest unclenched, not because the number was large but because the number existed at all. Moving wasn't a mood he was choosing. It was a line item. It had been counted, in 1967, by people with clipboards who had apparently watched enough teenagers drag boxes into empty rooms to decide the boxes were the problem.

"Twenty each," he said slowly, doing the arithmetic of his own life. "So I got both. A residence and a school." Kierra said the scale was for adults, originally, and that she didn't know if it even applied to him, and Mr. Santos-Reyes said from the doorway, where he'd been quietly collecting the empty dish, that in his experience anything a psychologist could measure, a teenager could double. Chase laughed harder than the line deserved.

Later, when they'd gone and the house had gone back to its cave-silence, he lay on the floor of what would be his bedroom and texted Camilo the thing about the twenty points, typing it out carefully, the year and the scale and the comparison, like evidence for a case he was still building. In his head he tried out an argument he'd been rehearsing since June: that leaving was fine because everything changes anyway, so it doesn't matter where you are. But that had started to sound tautological to him lately, a circle pretending to be a line, the conclusion just the premise wearing a hat. And there was the other way of thinking, Camilo's way, which was that place is the whole point, that the aquifer under their old neighborhood wasn't just geology, it was why the town existed, water under everything, invisible and load-bearing, like friendship. Chase didn't know yet if you could instantiate that kind of thing in a new town on purpose, or if it only ever happened by accident, over years, without anyone noticing. His phone buzzed. Camilo had replied with a picture of the frisbee's twin, the one he'd kept, balanced on his head like a hat, and one line: "Twenty points. Rookie numbers."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
Nicolas had the tassel threaded through his fingers like a worry stone by the time he reached the parking lot, where the June sun sat heavily on the hoods of a hundred cars and the asphalt smelled the way it always did after rain, like something steaming and unfinished. His gown was unzipped to the waist, cap shoved backward, and under his arm was a box of everything he had cleared out of his locker that morning: a frayed physics binder, a photo of the robotics team, a broken trophy he kept meaning to throw away. He set the box on the trunk of the Civic.

The Civic was the problem, or rather the Civic was where the problem lived. He and Carter had rebuilt it over two years in the corner of the school lot, in the space Mr. Vargas, the shop teacher, had quietly let them use after hours. They had pulled the engine in February, argued over the timing belt in March, and gotten it running on a cold Tuesday in April when Carter had whooped so loudly that a janitor came out to see who had been injured. The plan, stated a hundred times, was that they would drive it to State together in the fall, Nicolas to classes, Carter to the town nearby where his uncle had offered him work at the machine shop. Then, in May, Carter had told him he wasn't going. Not to the machine shop, not to anything near State. He was taking the job in the city instead, the one his mother wanted, the one with benefits, and he had said it all in one flat sentence while tightening a bolt and not looking up.

Nicolas had not said much since. He had said nothing at commencement, in fact, had pointedly not looked for Carter's row, and now the diploma in his gown pocket felt like a door closing on a hinge he had oiled himself.

"Nice ceremony," Drake said, arriving with his own gown balled under one arm. "Long, though. The valedictorian tried to problematize, like, everything. Social media, capitalism, the parking situation." He leaned on the fender. "You okay? You look like somebody stole your catalytic converter."

"Carter's not coming to the bonfire," Nicolas said. "He told me this morning. He's leaving tonight, actually. His mom wants to beat the traffic."

Drake whistled low. He picked up the broken trophy from the box and turned it over. "You two talk since he told you?"

"What is there to talk about. He made a decision."

"Man." Drake set the trophy down with exaggerated care, as if it were the matter itself and might shatter. "You know why they call it commencement? It means beginning. That's why they used the word for graduation, because graduates begin a new status, like bachelor or master." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, but he watched Nicolas while he said it.

"That's not germane," Nicolas said, though he noticed it landed anyway, somewhere under the ribs, the way a fact does when it arrives at the exact moment you have been insisting on the opposite. He had spent four days treating the ceremony as an ending, a funeral with better catering, and here was Drake handing him the genealogy of the word like it was nothing, like the whole apparatus of caps and gowns had been telling him the truth the entire time and he had refused the translation.

"It's germane to everything," Drake said. "Your boy's commencing too. Just not in your direction."

Mr. Vargas came out then, jingling the gate keys, because the corner of the lot where the Civic had lived was technically his to lock. He was the kind of teacher who never made speeches, which Nicolas had always appreciated, and he only said, "You moving it tonight or is it my lawn ornament for another summer?"

"Moving it," Nicolas said. Then, because the word was still working on him: "Actually, one more place first."

He drove. He knew the route to Carter's house the way he knew the feel of the clutch, without thinking, past the reservoir and the closed drive-in and the turn where the road went briefly to gravel. Carter was in the driveway loading boxes into his mother's sedan, and he straightened up when the Civic pulled in, and for a second neither of them did anything at all.

"I'm not good at this," Nicolas said, getting out. "I've been mad at you for picking a life."

"I know," Carter said. "I've been mad at me a little too."

"You could have told me why."

"I don't have a great why. There's no speech. It's just the one that made sense." Carter wiped his hands on his jeans. "You want to drive it one more time? Around the block."

They drove around the block twice, Carter in the passenger seat where he had spent two years not sitting, because he had always insisted on driving. The engine sounded clean. At the second stop sign Nicolas said, "I looked up the word once, commencement. Drake told me what it means and I told him it wasn't relevant, but he was right. It means beginning. The whole thing is named for starting a new status. Bachelor, master, whatever comes next."

"So we're both starting," Carter said. "It just doesn't look like it from here."

"It doesn't," Nicolas agreed. He pulled back into the driveway and left the engine running while Carter got out, and when Carter leaned back in the window he said, "Text me when you're settled. You still owe me half a timing belt."

"Mail it to me," Carter said. "I'll fix anything, forever, you know that." He tapped the roof twice, the old signal, and Nicolas pulled out onto the road with the windows down, the last light flat and gold across the reservoir, and drove toward the lot where the bonfire was already starting to glow.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: If air resistance is ignored, a projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acts on it.
story:
The ramp had been Cayden's father's idea, back when Cayden's father still had ideas about weekends, and it stood at the back fence like a boreal monument, grey and rain-split, taller than either of them remembered it being. Cole sat on the porch steps with a notebook open on his knee, a calculator balanced on the brick beside him, and tried to decide whether the question in front of him was stupid or only embarrassing.

"If you launch off the top," Corinne said, standing at the far end of the yard with a chalk line she'd drawn in the grass, "I'm saying you clear the garden bed. Cayden says you don't."

"I said I don't know," Cayden said. "That's different from saying I won't."

"You said forty dollars' worth of don't know."

Cole tuned them out, which had become easier over the summer, and looked at his numbers. The top of the ramp was 1.25 metres up. If he left it at four metres per second, the math he'd transcribed from the board in June gave him a flight time of about half a second. Half a second, four metres per second, and his pencil stopped moving, because he suddenly wasn't sure whether he was allowed to just multiply them.

In June he'd been sure, and being sure had cost him. Mr. Joseph had handed back the test with a red circle around Cole's answer, twelve metres, and beside it a single question mark that managed to be more insulting than any comment. Cole had gone up after class, and Mr. Joseph had said, "You treated the velocity like it slows down on the way through the air. It doesn't. If we ignore air resistance, the horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acts on it." He'd said it once, without looking up from his grading, and Cole had stood there feeling the sentence rearrange something in his head, like a door swinging open in a house he'd lived in for years without knowing the room existed.

Now he ran it again on the porch. Half a second of flight. Four metres per second, unchanging, the whole way, because nothing was pushing sideways on him once he left the ramp. Two metres. He looked out at the garden bed, at the chalk line Corinne had drawn, and at the metre and a half of grass between the two, and the answer sat in his stomach with a weight that had nothing to do with physics.

"Two metres," he said. "Give or take."

"You'll clear it," Corinne said immediately.

"Barely." He closed the notebook. "That's the problem with barely."

Cayden came and sat beside him on the steps, close enough that their shoulders touched, which Cayden did when he wanted to say something he hadn't decided how to say yet. Cole waited. The sprinkler two houses down made its slow ticking arc, and somewhere a lawnmower started and then thought better of it.

"Everything after the kick-off is in the air," Cole said. "There's no steering. That's what I keep landing on. You commit at the top and then physics just, finishes it for you."

"Is that about the ramp or about Friday?"

"About the ramp."

"Because I talked to her Thursday and she said she might come by tonight, and when I said you'd be here she said 'good' in a way that had at least three meanings."

Cole looked at the notebook again so he wouldn't have to look at Cayden. In the fall he'd be four hours north at a school nobody from their town had ever heard of, and Corinne would be at the state school, and Cayden would be here, working at his uncle's shop, and all summer Cole had been treating the distance like a solved problem, something you write down and box. The truth was he hadn't run the numbers at all. He'd just assumed the answer was no, because assuming no was easier than finding out.

"That's a lemma," Cayden said.

"A what?"

"From your own book, I read it over your shoulder at lunch. A thing you prove on the way to proving the real thing. Her showing up tonight is a lemma."

"You've been reading my math book for fun."

"I've been reading your math book for you." Cayden stood and pulled the skateboard out of the grass. "You going to ride the thing or just write a paper about it?"

Cole walked to the ramp. He put the board on the top, measured the drop with his eyes one more time, and did the only part of the math that mattered now: he committed. Four wheels, one push, the yard tilting upward as the ramp took him, and then the lip and the strange quiet of the air, half a second of it, exactly as calculated, during which nothing acted on him from the side at all and he was, for once in his life, going in a straight line he could not change.

He landed. The board wobbled, held, rolled. He put a foot down and looked back at the chalk line, at the garden bed, at the narrow stripe of uncut grass between them where his front wheel had come down, clean but only just.

From the porch, where Corinne had arrived without any of them noticing, her bike still ticking as it cooled against the railing, came a voice.

"So did you clear it or not?"

Cayden looked at Cole. Cole looked at the wheel print in the grass, and at her, and did not answer yet.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
The chicken had come out pale again. Henry stood at the steel counter of the school cooking classroom on a Thursday evening, staring at the tray of steamed thighs his family had politely eaten two nights before, and the memory of his mother sawing through a rubbery piece still made his ears go hot. Ms. Munro had given him a key to the room for the semester, one of those quiet arrangements adults make when they decide a kid needs somewhere to be, and he had promised them all a proper dinner on Sunday. That gave him three attempts.

Louis-Felix sat on a stool by the sink, eating crackers out of the box. "Just fry it," he said. "Nobody steams chicken unless they're in prison."

"It's what the recipe said." Henry turned the burner on and set the empty pan over it, the way his grandmother had told him to, pan hot first, then the oil, then the meat. She hadn't explained anything. She had only tapped the edge of the pan with a wooden spoon and said, "Hotter than you think," and gone back to her tea, leaving him to work out what hotter than you think actually meant.

Janessa came in carrying her own grocery bag, because she had volunteered to be the taste-tester and took the position seriously. She peered at his phone, where he had a notebook page open, and read over his shoulder. "Maillard reaction," she said, pointing at the phrase.

"That's the word." He had found it at one in the morning, scrolling through forums where people argued about pans the way other people argued about cars. The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor, and it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius. He had read it three times, then looked up the boiling point of water and understood, in a small cold flash, why his steamed chicken tasted like nothing at all. Steam could never get the pan where it needed to be. The whole dinner had been cooked in the wrong neighborhood of temperature, and no amount of salt afterward could fix that.

He dropped a bead of water into the pan. It skated around, hissing, and he lowered the chicken in skin-side down and was rewarded with a sound like applause. The skin began to color almost immediately, going gold, then amber at the edges, and the smell that rose up was so different from Thursday's bland steam that it felt like an argument being won.

"So it's just heat," Louis-Felix said, leaning in. "More heat, better food."

"It's the right heat." Henry was already worried about the other side of it, because the same pages warned about burning, about pushing past browning into char, and the line between them seemed narrow and unforgiving. There was something belligerent about the way the fat spat now, as if the pan resented being asked to do two things at once. He turned the piece early, then turned it back, not sure, and Janessa laughed at him.

"You're hovering."

"I'm calibrating." He checked the thermometer he had borrowed from the supply cabinet, the one Ms. Munro used for candy making. Not for the chicken itself but for the oil, to see whether he was somewhere inside that window or fooling himself. He worked the reading into his notebook next to the times and the results, because Sunday was coming whether he felt ready or not, and a promise made under that kind of duress had to be kept with something better than hope.

When the piece came out he set it on a rack instead of a plate, because the forums agreed about that too, and Janessa pulled it apart with two forks. The skin crackled. She went quiet in a way that was better than any compliment, and Louis-Felix took a piece without asking, which in his language was surrender.

"Same chicken as Thursday," Henry said, mostly to himself.

"No," Janessa said, mouth full. "Thursday was a rumor of chicken. This is chicken."

He wrote down the temperature, and under it a question he could not yet answer: how hot is too hot, before gold becomes black. The thermometer would tell him numbers, but the nose and the eye would have to learn the rest, and he did not know yet whether that was knowledge you could write down at all. He turned back to the stove and laid the next piece in, listening to it sizzle.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
The radiator under the window of Ms. Adeyemi's office ticked like something counting down, and Juliette kept her eyes on the folder in front of her because the poster behind Ms. Adeyemi's head said DECIDE WITH CONFIDENCE in letters that seemed to mock the whole hour. She had brought her draft, four hundred words about the summer she'd spent transcribing her grandmother's recipes into a taxonomy of emulsions, chemistry folded into memory, and she pushed it across the desk with the pride of someone offering something she was not sure would be taken.

Ms. Adeyemi read it the way a connoisseur reads a wine list, unhurried, with small movements of her chin, and Juliette watched for a verdict and got none. "This is good," Ms. Adeyemi said finally. "But which question is it answering?"

"Question?" Juliette said. "It's my personal statement. My cousin Dami wrote one just like it two years ago and got into Manchester. He said the trick is to braid the personal with the academic so the reader can't tell where one ends."

Ms. Adeyemi turned her monitor toward Juliette. On the screen was the UCAS page, and it did not say personal statement anywhere. It said, in the flat typeface of official forms, that starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS had replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions. One asked why the applicant wanted the subject. Another asked how they had prepared for it. Juliette read the third twice and felt the folder under her hand go from proof of work to evidence of a mistake.

"He didn't mention questions," she said. Her voice came out smaller than she intended. "He said one essay, open field, make yourself unforgettable."

"He applied in a different year," Ms. Adeyemi said, which was not an accusation but landed like one. She slid the draft back across the desk. "The deadline is Friday."

The word Friday sat in the room. Juliette looked at her four hundred words and understood, with a cold clarity, that the braided essay Dami had coached her through, the one she'd revised eleven times since September, no longer had a home. The form would not accept a braid. It wanted the strands separated: why chemistry, in one box; how prepared, in another. Somewhere behind the office door she could hear Emmanuel arguing with someone about a fixture list, Nathaniel's laugh rising over it, the ordinary noise of a school that did not know her whole architecture had just been rezoned.

She took out a pen and, on the back of the draft, drew three boxes. "The why is my grandmother's kitchen," she said, mostly to herself. "The how is the transcription project, the online course, the shadowing at the lab in Lille." It occurred to her that the new format was not only a loss. A free-form statement rewarded people who had been taught the genre, who had cousins and coaches and parents who knew the unwritten rules; a structured question told you exactly what was being asked. It was harder to be disenfranchised by a form that showed you its own skeleton. And yet something ductile in the old essay, the part where her grandmother's hands and the chemistry of emulsions became one thing, might not survive being sorted into boxes. She could see the value of both systems at once, and she could not make them agree.

"Can I keep some of the braid inside a question?" she asked.

"That depends on whether it answers what's asked," Ms. Adeyemi said, and picked up her pen as well. "Show me where you'd cut."

Juliette drew a line through the first paragraph, then stopped with the pen resting on the sentence about her grandmother's hands, the one she could not yet bring herself to strike. The radiator ticked. Outside, a bell rang and Emmanuel's voice moved away down the corridor. She crossed out the sentence, then wrote it again in the margin of the first box, smaller, in the space where the letters could still almost fit, and slid the page back across the desk toward Ms. Adeyemi's waiting hand.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice.
story:
The folding chairs in the town hall gymnasium had been arranged in crooked rows, and Maelle chose one near the back where she could see both the podium and the door. She had come because her civics teacher had offered extra credit for attending a public forum on the county charter, but she stayed because Jacob waved her over to a seat beside him and Angelina, who were already arguing about something.

"Tell her," Angelina said, jabbing a thumb at Jacob. "Tell her a president should be allowed to run as many times as he wants. If people keep voting for him, that's democracy."

"That's not what I said," Jacob protested, but the moderator, a narrow man in a gray suit, tapped the microphone and the room went quiescent, all that loose chatter settling into attention at once.

The charter debate itself was dull, something about drainage easements, and Maelle felt her mind drift. She had spent the whole week confused in Mr. Suzuki's class, where they were comparing how different countries choose and fire their leaders. In a parliamentary system, she understood now, the head of government was chosen by the legislature and could be removed by a vote of no confidence, which meant a prime minister could fall in an afternoon. In a presidential system, the president was elected separately and, short of impeachment, was nearly impossible to dislodge before the term ended. Two logics, one built on constant accountability, the other on stability. She could recite both. She could not yet say which she actually believed, and that gap bothered her like a stone in her shoe.

During the open comment period, a farmer in a seed cap stood up and said the county supervisor should serve as long as the voters kept choosing him, term limits be damned. "Why should a piece of paper tell the people when to stop voting for a good man?"

"That's what I said," Jacob whispered, delighted.

Angelina leaned across him toward Maelle. "You're taking Suzuki's class. Set him straight."

Maelle hesitated. She thought of the diagram Mr. Suzuki had sketched on the board, the two boxes, the arrows. "It's not that simple," she said quietly. "In the American system, the Twenty-second Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice. It doesn't matter how popular he is. The rule is the rule."

"So the people can be wrong for eight straight years and the paper knows better?" Jacob said.

"No, it's that power doesn't stay benign just because it started that way," Maelle said, surprising herself with her own firmness. "But the parliamentary side has its own problem. A prime minister with a shaky majority can be gone in weeks, and then the whole government is unstable." She paused. "I used to think one system was just better. Now I think you're choosing which failure you'd rather guard against."

Mr. Suzuki, who turned out to be three rows ahead with a clipboard, turned around in his chair. "That's the beginning of an actual position, Maelle. Which failure would you rather guard against?"

Everyone nearby was listening now, the farmer included, and Maelle felt her face warm. "I don't know yet," she admitted. "Maybe you want stability when things are calm and accountability when they're not. But I can't figure out how a constitution would know the difference."

"Homeostasis," Mr. Suzuki said, smiling. "A system that corrects itself."

"Except sometimes it overcorrects," Angelina said. "Or it doesn't correct at all, and the problem just metastasizes, spreads into everything, and by the time you notice, it's the whole government."

The moderator called the comment period back to order, and the drainage easements resumed, and Maelle sat with her hands folded, running through the argument again in her head. She had given both systems their due and arrived not at an answer but at a sharper question, which felt, she thought, like progress of a kind nobody hands out extra credit for.

Afterward, in the parking lot under the sodium lights, Jacob caught up with her. "So if a prime minister can lose his job in one bad vote, and a president is locked in unless you impeach him, which one would you actually live under?"

Maelle pulled her jacket tighter against the cold. "Ask me again after I've voted in something," she said, and opened the car door.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Accounting profit subtracts only money actually paid out, while economic profit also subtracts implicit costs such as the owner's time and the next-best use of their money.
story:
The Saturday shift at the garden center began, as it always did, with the misting of the ferns. Brody worked the nozzle down the aisle in a slow sweep, and the water beaded on the leaves and ran onto the concrete floor, darkening it in long streaks. Behind the register, Ms. Joseph counted the drawer with the patience of someone who had counted ten thousand drawers. The morning light came through the greenhouse plastic in a flat white sheet, and the whole store had the smell of wet soil and cold metal.

Lennon arrived at eleven, the way she did most Saturdays, because the greenhouse sat four doors from her house and because her mother wanted her out from under the ceiling fan where she packed orders. She carried a shoebox under one arm and set it on the potting bench beside Brody.

"Look at this," she said. She opened the lid. Inside, stacked in neat columns, were the small succulent cuttings she sold online, their fat leaves dusted with the fine grit she grew them in. "Twenty-six orders this month. I cleared three hundred and forty dollars after the pots and the soil and the shipping. Three hundred and forty, Brody."

"That's real money," he said, and it was. He made a hundred and sixty a week here and it took him twenty hours to get it.

She lingered while he moved the shoebox to the back shelf where the sun wouldn't reach it, and while he hauled a new bale of substrate to the potting station and cut the twine and broke it apart with his hands. The compressed block crumbled into something dark and loose. Lennon watched him work and talked the whole time, about a girl in her chemistry class who had started reselling thrifted dresses, about whether the cuttings would root faster under a grow light.

The afternoon had a glacial pace after she left. Brody swept, restacked terracotta pots, and stood at the register while a man argued for ten minutes about whether a dead hydrangea could be returned. Ms. Joseph refunded him without any change in her face. Around four, when the store went empty, she came and stood beside Brody at the window and said, "Your friend with the box. Is that her little business?" He said it was. "She tells me she's making money," Ms. Joseph said, and then she went back to the ledgers she kept in the back room, and left him with the sentence, which sat strangely in his mind, because it had sounded less like praise than like a question.

He thought about it while he rang up a woman buying seed trays. Lennon had said three hundred and forty dollars after the pots and the soil and the shipping. He found himself doing the arithmetic in his head while he bagged the trays. He knew her schedule better than almost anyone's. She spent her lunch period packing orders in the art room. She gave up her Saturdays. He had watched her cancel on the lake trip in June because a batch had to be repotted. He started counting hours the way he counted change, and the count would not stop at a tidy number. Two hours a night, easily, most nights, and a Saturday here and there, and the time she spent driving to the post office on the far side of town.

On Monday after school he sat on the wall outside the library with his phone out and worked it as a word problem, the kind Ms. Joseph might put in front of him if she taught anything besides plants. Suppose Lennon paid herself nothing. Then her three hundred and forty dollars was what was left when you subtracted only the money she had actually handed over, for pots and soil and shipping and tape. But she had handed over something else that never appeared on any receipt. She had handed over her own hours, dozens of them, and if she had worked those hours here at the garden center at minimum wage she would have earned more than the business paid her. There was a word for the two ways of seeing it, and he half remembered it from a business elective his brother had left a textbook behind for, something about accounting versus economic profit. One counted the money out the door. The other counted the money out the door and the things you gave up that never showed up on a door at all, your own time, and whatever else your hours or your savings could have been doing instead.

He texted Lennon and asked her straight out how many hours. She wrote back "lol why," and then, a minute later, "maybe 45?" Forty-five hours for three hundred and forty dollars came to less than eight an hour, and the state's minimum was higher than that, and he knew it because he was paid it.

He walked to her house on Thursday. She was at the kitchen table with the shoebox open, wrapping a cutting in damp paper towel, and he told her the numbers, quietly, the way you hand someone a fragile thing. She kept wrapping. She taped the paper and wrote the address on the label and did not look up for a while.

"So it's economic profit," she said finally, tapping the label against the table edge. "Or the lack of it." She held the parcel out toward him as if it were evidence. "Forty-five hours. I never once wrote those down."

He said, "You don't have to stop."

"I know I don't." She set the parcel on the stack with the others, squaring its corner against the one below it. "But tomorrow I'm pricing my time before I price the pots."

Outside, the sprinklers had come on across her lawn, and the two of them stood watching the water arc and fall through the last of the light.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A LEFT JOIN in SQL returns every row from the left table, filling the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row exists.
story:
The summer course cost forty dollars, money Sienna had earned by dog walking, and she had promised herself she would finish it before orientation in August. Her laptop sat open on the kitchen table, the fan clicking in a way it had learned over the years, and on the screen were two tables she had invented herself: customers and orders. She had imagined a small shop, the kind her mother liked, selling candles and honey, and she had populated the customers table with names borrowed from people she knew. Jessica had ordered twice. Mahmoud had ordered once, a jar of clover honey, in June. Her mother, entered simply as "Mom," had ordered nothing at all, because in Sienna's small economy mothers got things for free.

The assignment asked a question that seemed almost too plain to be the point of a whole lesson: which customers had never ordered anything? Sienna had tried a plain JOIN first, the ordinary kind, and stared at the result. Jessica appeared twice, Mahmoud once, and the others, eleven rows of them, had simply vanished. She scrolled down as though they might be hiding below the fold of the screen, then scrolled back up. It felt like a class photo where only the loud kids showed up.

She opened a message to Mahmoud, who was taking the same course across town, and typed, "When you join customers to orders, does your list lose people?" His reply came as three dots that lasted long enough for her to get water from the tap. Then: "Yeah. Mine too. Only people who bought stuff." He added, "Try the other one. The uppercase one from the video." He had a sardonic way of referring to the instructor, a man who wore the same gray shirt in every lesson and said "elegant" about queries the way other people said it about bridges.

The other one was LEFT JOIN. Sienna typed it carefully, left table first, and ran it, and the whole roster came back: thirteen rows, every single customer, Jessica twice, Mahmoud once. But the rows for the quiet customers looked strange. Where the order numbers and dates should have been, the screen said NULL, in small pale letters, again and again, like a word repeated in a language she didn't yet speak. She sat back. So that was the trick. A LEFT JOIN kept every row from the left table and filled the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row existed. The empty people hadn't disappeared; they had been marked.

"NULL means no order," Mahmoud wrote when she told him. "It's how the empty shows up."

She ran her finger down the column of NULLs and felt a small, unaccountable gladness. The question at the bottom of the lesson asked her to identify the non-buyers, and she could do it now: Mom, and a neighbor she'd entered as Ms. Njoroge, the retired teacher from two floors down who sometimes held the door with her cane and asked what Sienna was reading. The query had found them by noticing their absence, which seemed like a strange power for a machine to have. She wondered how many other things could be found this way, by looking for what wasn't there.

Then the extension question caught her, the one labeled "for the ambitious": the shop owner wanted to email the non-buyers a coupon, ten percent off, to bring them back. Sienna read it twice. It was harmless, obviously. A coupon. But something in it reminded her of the videos her cousin watched about how to monetize an audience, the phrase itself, "monetize," turning people into a number with a dollar sign in front of it. The NULL rows had felt almost tender a minute ago, a way of remembering the forgotten. Now they were a mailing list.

She got up and stood at the window over the parking lot. The trouble wasn't the query. The query had a kind of rectitude to it, actually, a plainness about what it kept and what it marked; it told the truth about absence and nothing else. The trouble was what you did next. If she wrote the coupon query, she would be deciding that the people who ordered nothing were a problem to be solved rather than people who simply, for their own reasons, at their own pace, hadn't gotten around to honey. Maybe both things were true. Maybe Ms. Njoroge would like a coupon. Maybe she would find it presumptuous, an assumption that everyone was waiting to be nudged.

The gray-shirted instructor had not covered any of this. The lesson ended at the query, as though the list were the destination, and Sienna suspected that most of the world's lists ended the same way, delivered to someone who never had to think about the NULLs at all. She carried the thought back to the table with her cold glass.

She wrote the coupon query anyway, saved it in a file, and then, before closing the laptop, created a second file beside it: the same thirteen rows, the same quiet NULLs, no coupon, no email, just the names. She left both files on the desktop, side by side, and looked at them for a moment. Then she opened the message to Mahmoud and typed, "Did you do the coupon part?"

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
Felix had promised himself he would do it over breakfast, so the article lay open on the kitchen table between his cereal bowl and his mother's newspaper, and he was losing to both of them. The article was in Portuguese, which he had been studying for exactly four months, and it was supposed to be short, which it was, in the way a small door can still open onto a large dark room. The assignment, due in Mr. Charles's class tomorrow morning, was simple: read a short news article in your new language and summarise it aloud, two minutes, no notes. He had chosen one about a city banning e-scooters from its bike lanes, and it had seemed manageable right up until the third paragraph.

"You're making a face," his mother said, pouring coffee. "The same face you made during tax season."

"That was amortize face. This is different. This is a man named Ricardo who is apparently furious about micromobility, and I know maybe half his words."

Junior had sent him three texts that morning, each more relaxed than the last. i picked a weather article lol. weather has like forty words total. Felix had picked the scooter article because it felt incisive, because it argued something, and now he sat there parsing it word by word like a ransom note. He typed back: how many words do you actually know in yours. Junior replied with a shrug emoji, which was an answer in itself, the way a shrug always is.

He tried reading a paragraph aloud and heard himself stop, start, stop, like a car learning a clutch. Every sentence had one or two words that snagged him, and each snagged word dragged the whole sentence into guesswork. He looked up " concessionária" and then, three lines later, "desde já," and then a phrase about "the responsible party" that he assembled from context and prayer. His mother watched him over her mug with open amusement. "Is that Portuguese or are you having a small medical event?"

"It's a small medical event conducted in Portuguese."

He called Shayne, who was in the same class and had, annoyingly, grown up with a Brazilian grandmother. "Ask me something," he said when she picked up. "Ask me what the article is about."

"Okay. What is the article about?"

"A city... did a thing... to scooters... in lanes that are for... bicycles." He could hear her not laughing, which was worse than laughing.

"Did you count how many words you actually know in it?" she asked. She sounded genuinely curious, not smug, which was the most Shayne thing about her. "Because I read something once, this linguist, Paul Nation, research he did with colleagues. They found readers need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help."

"Ninety-eight," Felix said.

"So if it feels like a puzzle, it's not because you're bad at it. Do the math on your paragraph."

He hung up, took his pen, and marked the third paragraph: forty-three words, three he didn't know. He did it twice because the arithmetic felt personal. That was nowhere near ninety-eight percent; it was ninety-three, and the missing seven percent were doing something out of proportion to their size, like the two grams of salt that decide whether soup is soup. He had been treating the article like a test of character when it was actually a test of selection.
