His subterfuge of pretending the difficulty was virtuous collapsed on the spot, and it was almost a relief to let it.

He went back to the news site and scrolled past the scooter article, feeling briefly like a quitter, then less so. He found a shorter piece about a library reopening after a flood. He counted its first paragraph: fifty-two words, one unknown. He counted the second: one again. He estimated the whole thing at ninety-eight, maybe a hair better, and read it through once without stopping, which was a sensation he hadn't had in Portuguese before, like water going down smoothly instead of in gulps.

He practised the summary aloud in the kitchen while his mother pretended to read her newspaper and corrected his pronunciation of "biblioteca" twice, having no Portuguese at all but strong convictions. "The library," he said, pacing, "was closed eight months after the water, and the people, the community, they brought back... they donated more books than they lost." His mother lowered the paper. "That's actually a nicer story than scooters."

"Mr. Charles never said it had to be a fight."

He texted Junior: keep your weather article, but count your words, ninety-eight percent is the number, and left it at that, because Junior would either do the math or he wouldn't. Then he stood at the counter and ran the summary once more, timing it on the stove clock, and when it came in at one minute fifty, he said "biblioteca" one last time, carefully, the way you'd set down something you didn't want to chip.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: A coda is an optional closing section after the recapitulation that reinforces the home key and brings the movement to an end.
story:
Matthew spread the photocopy across the kitchen table and weighted its corners with two mugs and a butter dish. The score was Mozart's Piano Sonata in F, K. 332, first movement, shrunk to eight pages by a cheap copier until the sixteenth notes looked like splinters. On Monday, Ms. Abdi had told the class to mark the exposition, the development and the recapitulation in coloured pencil, and to bring the result to the lesson on Thursday. She had said nothing else. That silence was the assignment, as far as Matthew could tell.

He had started confidently. The exposition announced itself: first theme in F major, second theme in the dominant, a clean change of key that even his embryonic ear could hear as a shift of light. He bracketed it in blue and wrote "EXPOSITION" in handwriting that he hoped looked unhurried. The development was easier still, because it was chaos by design, fragments of theme thrown into distant keys, and he marked its beginning in red at the first real stumble of harmony.

The recapitulation he found by humming, playing the opening theme back to himself until he met it again, returning home like the same street seen from the opposite direction. Green pencil, thick bracket, a small triumphant note in the margin. Then he sat back and looked at what remained: a page and a half of music that his three colours did not cover. His markings ran out before the music did.

His mother drifted through for coffee and paused at his shoulder. "Homework with pictures," she said. "Better than your chemistry." She tapped the leftover passage. "What's this bit?" He said he didn't know yet, and she carried her cup away, satisfied with an answer that sounded like one.

He texted Denis first, but Denis had marked only up to the recapitulation and stopped there, on the theory that whatever Ms. Abdi hadn't named didn't need naming. That was Denis's whole philosophy of school, and of most things. Karan answered on the second try, his voice arriving tinny and close, as though he were speaking from inside a locker. "Everyone in our group hit the same wall. The markings finish and Mozart keeps going." Karan wanted more than the right answer, Matthew knew; he wanted to be the one who found it, so that Ms. Abdi would finally put him in the chamber group for the spring concert instead of the second violinist she kept promising it to. "Come over," Matthew said. "Bring your phone, the recording's on it."

They listened at the kitchen table with one earbud each, following the score with their fingers. After the green recapitulation ended, the music did something Matthew could only describe as insisting. The F major chords came back and back, emphatic, rounded, final in a way the recapitulation itself had not been. "It's still in F," Karan said. "Same key as the start. Like it's proving it's finished." Matthew looked at the closing bars, the repeated chords stacked like sandbags. The passage was optional, he realised, in the way a signature is optional on a letter; the movement could have ended at the recapitulation and made sense, but this ending made it certain.

"I looked it up after rehearsal," Karan said, a little too casually. "It's called a coda." He said the word quickly, then leaned over Matthew's pencilled pages. "You do the marks. I want the labels neat, Ms. Abdi hates my writing." Matthew took the orange pencil and drew the fourth bracket, wrote CODA beside it, and under it, smaller, not certain enough to leave out: "closing section, after the recapitulation, ends in the home key." The consonance of the two boys at one table, each holding half of the answer, felt more durable than either half alone. He was not sure his four brackets were right; he was not even sure Thursday would settle it, since Ms. Abdi seemed to treat certainty itself as something to be questioned. But he had gone from three colours to four, and from stopping where his system stopped to asking what the music was doing past the edge of it.

His mother looked in again on her way to bed. "Solved your extra bit?" "Mostly," Matthew said. Karan snapped the pencil case shut, and the orange pencil rolled off the table and across the floor, coming to rest against the butter dish.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Jewish law, the principle of pikuach nefesh holds that saving a human life overrides almost every other commandment, including the rules of the Sabbath.
story:
The debate topic had been assigned on Wednesday, and by Friday evening Laura still had no case. Resolved: that ancient religious rules cannot govern modern life. She was arguing the negative, which meant she had to defend rules she didn't fully understand, and Mr. Bouchard had made it clear he would fail any argument that leaned on vague reverence. "Use the text itself," he had said, tapping the whiteboard. "Or don't bother."

She had come to her grandmother's house for the quiet, and for the bookshelf in the study, which held her grandfather's commentaries in worn blue and green volumes. David had texted her a prolix summary of secular counterarguments, three screens of scrolling text that said, in the end, only that modern people know better. Genevieve had sent a single line: "Find something in there that actually bites."

At Friday night dinner her grandmother mentioned, between complaints about the neighbor's hedge, that she had felt dizzy all afternoon. Laura's mother told her to sit down. The grandmother said she was fine, that dizziness at eighty-two did not portend anything, and then she stood to clear the plates and the room tilted, and Laura caught her elbow before she reached the floor.

They laid her on the couch. Her color was wrong, gray under the lamp light, and she kept insisting she only needed to rest. Laura's mother stood in the middle of the room with her coat half on and her keys in her fist, and did not move.

"I can't," her mother said. "I can't drive. It's Shabbos."

"Mom, she's sick."

"I know she's sick." The keys rattled in her hand. Laura had never heard her mother's voice go thin like that, torn between two things she believed.

Laura went back to the study. She was looking for anything, a phone number, a pamphlet, and she pulled down the index volume her grandfather had annotated in pencil and ran her finger down the columns. There it was, a cross-reference in his cramped hand, and under it a page in another commentary marked with a torn strip of paper towel. She read the paragraph twice. Saving a human life, it said, overrides almost every other commandment, including the rules of the Sabbath. Not in the loose way people say rules were made to be broken. The obligation ran the other way. You were required to break the Sabbath to save a life.

She carried the book out to the living room, open, and put it on the coffee table in front of her mother.

"Read this part. Grandpa marked it."

Her mother read. She put two fingers on the page as if checking it was real.

"Pikuach nefesh," the grandmother said from the couch, without opening her eyes. "Your grandfather loved that one. Life comes first."

"Almost every commandment," Laura said, pointing at the line. "Including the Sabbath. It says you have to."

Her mother looked at the book, then at her own mother, then at Laura, and something in her face let go of the argument she'd been having with herself. She knelt, got the grandmother's shoes on, took her arm, and walked her to the car in the dark. Laura watched the taillights go down the long driveway and turn toward the hospital, twenty minutes away, and then she sat down on the couch with the commentary still open on her knees.

She wrote her case that night while she waited. She wrote that a tradition which builds its own escape hatch into its strictest rule is not naive about modern life; it has been thinking about emergencies longer than any of us. She wrote about her grandfather's pencil marks. She also, because Mr. Bouchard would ask, wrote the honest counterweight: that "almost" was doing enormous work in that sentence, that people would fight forever about where the line fell, and that she did not know, sitting there at one in the morning, whether her mother would have driven without the text. Maybe love alone would have been enough. The book had not created the mercy. It had only given her mother permission she already wanted.

At two the phone rang. Stable, her mother said, dehydration and a heart medication that needed adjusting, they were keeping her overnight. Laura said okay twice, and after she hung up she read the last page of her notes and deleted the final paragraph, the tidy one about what it all meant. Genevieve was right. It bit, and she would let it bite.

At the debate on Saturday morning she stood up with her index cards and the commentary in her bag, and opened with the line she had chosen at the kitchen table while the kettle clicked: "Last night my mother drove my grandmother to the hospital on the Sabbath, because the tradition itself told her to."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
Noemie sat in the driver's seat of her mother's car with her hands at ten and two, and her father in the passenger seat still holding the keys, which seemed to her a kind of argument in itself. The driveway sloped gently toward the street. Behind them, the garage door was open like a mouth. She had waited all winter for this, and now that the afternoon had actually arrived she kept thinking about Matilda, who had passed her test in October and had told Noemie, over fries at the place on Ridge Road, that the following distance thing was overblown. Two seconds, Matilda had said. Everyone says two seconds. My instructor was canny about everything else, but two seconds is what people actually do.

Her father finally handed over the keys. "Back out slowly," he said. "Then left, and we'll do the loop around the block."

Noemie turned the key. The engine caught, the car shivered once, and she reversed out of the driveway with the wheel turned too early so that the rear tire rode up over the curb and came down again with a soft thud. Her father didn't say anything, which was worse than if he had. She pulled the door mirror back into position with her finger and put the car in drive.

The first block went well enough. Then the car ahead of them, a silver hatchback with a dented bumper, slowed for no reason she could see, and Noemie braked harder than she meant to. Her father braced one hand against the dash. "Give yourself three seconds," he said. "Watch the car in front pass something fixed, a sign, a shadow, and count before you reach it. Three seconds minimum, and add one more for anything difficult. Rain, heavy traffic, that's another second each."

"That's a lot of room," Noemie said. "Matilda says two."

"Matilda can drive however she likes," her father said, and looked out the window.

They came around the block and back into the neighborhood, and Noemie tried it. When the hatchback passed a storm drain she started counting under her breath, one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three, and she was still two car lengths back when she finished. It felt excessive, almost rude, like standing too far from someone at a party. But when the hatchback braked again at the corner where the stop sign was half hidden by a hedge, she had already slowed before her foot even moved. She noticed that. She noticed that she hadn't had to decide anything.

That night she texted Matilda from the kitchen counter, and Matilda's reply sat on the screen like a letter she'd drafted three times: "ok so I looked it up bc my uncle had opinions and it's actually the National Safety Council, 3 seconds minimum and you add a second for every difficulty like rain or heavy traffic. I've basically been instantiating the wrong rule for eight months. don't tell Colin." Below that, a second message: "also it rained all day where you are right?? so add the second. the whole road is basically a different biome." Noemie laughed, then stopped laughing, because Matilda had been driving on two seconds through a whole Ohio winter, and because it was strange to think that a rule could live inside you, quietly wrong, and only announce itself when someone finally checked.

The next afternoon her father was at work, so Noemie walked out to the driveway with the keys on her own authority and just sat in the parked car, not going anywhere. The driveway sloped toward the street, and past the street was the cul-de-sac, and past that the road to school where the traffic stacked up at 7:40 every morning, eight minutes of brake lights, which she now understood counted as a difficulty, which meant four seconds, which meant she would be the car everyone changed lanes to get around. Two perspectives, both real to her: Matilda's, honed by eight months of actual driving, and the Council's, written by people who had presumably counted crashes. Noemie could not make them into one thing, and she was honest with herself about that. What she did have was the storm drain trick, the counting, the strange calm of having room before she needed it.

She started the car and backed out of the driveway, straighter this time, the tires missing the curb by a full hand's width. At the end of the street she stopped at the hidden sign, counted one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three, and then, because the sky had gone the color of wet slate, one thousand four.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
Audrey had failed the biology test on transcription and translation, and Ms. Ortiz, whose farm she worked at on Saturday mornings, had agreed to pay her for the usual chores anyway, in the same cash folded into an envelope, as though the failure were a private matter between Audrey and the county. The retake was Monday. She carried the textbook out to the kidding barn because the house was too quiet and the barn smelled of straw and iodine, which was better than smelling of nothing.

Kayleb was already there, sitting on an overturned feed bucket with his phone, waiting for his mother to finish the vet call in the back paddock. "You got the retake too?" he asked. "Dayne passed with a ninety. He made flashcards. I made a sandwich."

"I made a sandwich too," Audrey said. "Then I read the chapter twice and it fell apart both times."

The chapter kept its words at a distance from her. DNA unzipped, letters were copied into messenger RNA, and then something read the copy and produced protein, and somewhere in the middle of it all the book used the word ribosome and expected her to already feel what a ribosome was. She read the sentence aloud in the barn and the sentence lay there. Kayleb was doing something with baling twine, tying and untying the same knot.

Ms. Ortiz came through with a bucket of colostrum and stopped when she heard the word protein. "My mother could explain that whole thing with a loom," she said. "She never finished school. But I'm not going to explain it to you, because you'll remember what you build and forget what you're told." She set the bucket down. "Come with me first. The milking's done but the line needs flushing, and you two can help while you talk."

The pipeline in the parlour ran along the wall above the stalls, and when Ms. Ortiz opened the valve the rinse water pushed through and the machine pushed out a plug of leftover milk fat at the far end, a pale rope that came out steady and continuous, like dough through a die. "Extrude," Ms. Ortiz said, nodding at it. "That's the word for when a machine pushes something out through a shape. Remember that one, it's worth knowing." Then she left them to it.

Kayleb picked up the twine he'd been carrying and a handful of washers from the jar on the shelf by the pump, and sat down on the parlour step. "Okay, tell me the part you don't get," he said. "I'll tell you the part I don't get, which is all of it."

"Translation," Audrey said. "The last part. The copy gets read and a protein comes out, and the book makes it sound like magic."

Kayleb threaded a washer onto the twine. Then another. He held the twine taut and slid the washers along it one at a time, reading off a smudged photocopy of his notes that he'd pulled from his jacket pocket, and he said, "My cousin does this with beads. She reads the pattern off the paper and threads them in order, and at the end there's a bracelet. So the copy is the pattern." He slid the next washer. "And this thing reading it, the ribosome, that's her. It moves along the pattern, like my fingers moving along the string, and every bead it adds is an amino acid."

Audrey watched his fingers. The washers clicked against each other as the row grew, and she took the notes from him and found the line that had defeated her twice, and this time it moved. The ribosome travels along the messenger RNA, she read, and as it goes it joins the amino acids together, and the bonds that hold them to each other are called peptide bonds, and the chain it builds is the protein. That was the whole thing. Not magic. A reader moving down a pattern, adding units, linking them, and the finished chain coming off the end the way the fat had come out of the pipeline, one long continuous thing produced by a steady process.

"Say the whole part back to me," Kayleb said. "Ms. Ortiz said she'd quiz us at lunch."

"In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain," Audrey said, and as she said it her hand moved along the twine, thumb and finger travelling the string and pinching each washer to the last, and the row of washers stood up off her palm as a single stiff strand. Kayleb added a washer and the strand got longer by exactly one unit, and nothing about that was mysterious anymore.

They walked back up through the yard for lunch, and Kayleb asked whether the washers were really the amino acids or just a way of thinking about them, and Audrey said both, probably, or maybe the comparison was equivocal, that it worked and didn't work at the same time, and that she still couldn't picture how the first copy got made from the DNA in the first place, the transcription half of it, which the chapter had covered and which she had read and which still sat in her like a sealed room. "I'll know the one thing solidly and the other thing not at all," she said.

"Dayne would say just memorize it," Kayleb said.

"Dayne would," Audrey said. "Dayne treats the textbook like a magistrate, like it hands down rulings and you keep your head down and obey." She thought about that while they crossed the yard, and decided it was partly fair and partly an excuse, because a magistrate at least tells you the law, whereas the book had told her and she had simply not yet heard it. She went into the kitchen, washed her hands at the sink, and while the water ran she said the sentence about the ribosome once more under her breath, her thumb moving along the edge of the counter like a finger along a string.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 1904 physicist Robert W. Wood secretly removed a key prism from René Blondlot's apparatus, yet observers still reported seeing Blondlot's claimed 'N-rays', showing they were seeing what they expected.
story:
Ella opened the shared lab file at her desk and saw, in the third row, that Shiloh had already filled in the results. The assignment was a diffraction lab: measure the spacing of the fringes, record the numbers, and compare them against the predicted values. Ella had done her run on Tuesday without looking at the theory first, because Ms. Rivera had suggested it, and her table was a scatter of points that wandered off the line in a way she couldn't explain. Shiloh's table, completed last night, sat neatly along the prediction like beads on a string.

"You already did it," Ella said, because Shiloh's icon was green, which meant she was online, which meant the call was already ringing before Ella had decided to make it.

"I read the chapter first," Shiloh said. Her camera showed a kitchen, and behind her a younger brother was constructing some epicurean midnight snack, layering cheese on crackers with the concentration of a jeweler. "Once you know what the fringe spacing is supposed to be, it's easier to see where to measure. The numbers just come out cleaner." She said it the way people say things they suspect might not hold up. "Yours look rough."

"Mine look honest," Ella said, and immediately regretted the word, because it implied something about Shiloh's, and Shiloh's face did the small closing thing it did when she felt accused. They had been friends since the group project in ninth grade, and Ella knew the difference between Shiloh defending herself and Shiloh deciding whether to.

"I didn't make anything up," Shiloh said. "I measured what I saw."

Ella pulled up the search bar. She typed "seeing results you expect" and then, when that gave her self-help articles, "physics experiment expected results observers." She skimmed past a forum argument and a Wikipedia disambiguation page, and then she found it, on a page about something called N-rays, and she read the paragraph twice while Shiloh waited, audibly eating a grape.

"Listen to this," Ella said. "In 1904 a physicist named Robert W. Wood went to René Blondlot's lab in Nancy and secretly removed a key prism from the apparatus. The prism was supposed to be making the N-rays visible. And the observers still reported seeing them. They kept seeing what they expected to see, with the part that made it possible gone."

"That's horrifying," Shiloh said, without any horror in her voice, more like interest. "So the whole thing was a contrivance? The rays never existed?"

"The rays never existed," Ella said. "That's what the page says. But the people weren't lying. They believed it, and belief did the seeing." She looked back at her own crooked scatter of points, which suddenly looked less like failure. Then she looked at Shiloh's smooth line, and she understood that she couldn't tell, from the outside, which of them it described, and that this was the actual problem, bigger than one lab.

"So what do we do," Shiloh said. "Delete my numbers?"

Deleting them would be quick, surgical, a way to cauterize the disagreement before it spread into the writeup and the grade. Ella's hand was on the trackpad already. But Shiloh had measured what she saw; that was the whole point. The numbers weren't false, they were contaminated, in the way tap water is still water.

"Ms. Rivera said she'd accept two data sets," Ella said slowly. "She said one reason we work in pairs is that two people measuring the same thing is worth more than one person measuring it twice." She had assumed that was about workload. "What if we submit both, and the writeup is about why they're different?"

"They'll think I fudged it."

"They'll think one of us saw what she expected. The page says that's why other people tried to replicate, that's how the whole field decides anything. Not one result. Lots of people, lots of tries." Ella heard the younger brother's plate scrape somewhere off-camera, and the low sound of a parent's voice calling him to bed, and Shiloh turned her head to answer, then turned back.

"Fine," Shiloh said. "Both tables. But I'm writing the paragraph about my data, and you can write the one about yours, and we put the N-ray thing in the discussion where Rivera can't miss it." She was already copying her rows into a fresh sheet, and she paused, cursor blinking. "Wood, 1904. Spell the French guy's name for me."

"Blondlot," Ella said. "B-l-o-n-d-l-o-t."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In the recapitulation, the second theme usually returns in the home key rather than the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began.
story:
The music room smelled like radiator dust and old cork, and Tristan had been telling himself for a week that he didn't need help, which was one of those things he said so often it had begun to sound like a lie told politely. He spread the score of the Mozart sonata movement across the upright piano's lid and put a pencil down beside it, then moved the pencil to the other side, then back, because the placement of a pencil was apparently something he could control while the analysis was not. Ms. Sultani wanted the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation marked by Friday, with bars numbered and themes named, and he had spent three evenings circling things that turned out to be wrong.

"You're doing the thing," said Aryan from the doorway, cello case dragging behind him like a stubborn animal. "The thing where you stare at it until it apologizes."

"It's not going to apologize. It's going to make sense." Tristan slid over on the bench. "Sit. You actually read music."

Aryan sat, popped the score straight, and ran a finger down the first page. "Okay, exposition starts here, obviously, first theme in the home key, whole forte section. Then it goes to the dominant for the second theme, that's the whole point of an exposition, you move. Then development." He tapped a brace. "This part is just Mozart taking the themes apart and being obstreperous with them, wandering everywhere. Then recap, first theme comes back, and."

"And what," Tristan said, but he was already looking, because there was something he'd noticed the night before and dismissed, the way he dismissed most things he noticed after ten o'clock. The second theme, the one he loved, the lilting little tune that had made him pick this movement in the first place, appeared twice in the score. Once in the exposition. Once near the end. And the key signatures were different.

"Wait." He put his pencil on the first occurrence, then the second. "Look. Same theme, both places. But here it's in the dominant, and here, at the recapitulation, it's back in the home key." He said it slowly, testing it. "So it comes back but it doesn't come back the same. It comes back settled. In the key where the whole movement started."

Aryan leaned in. Jacey appeared in the doorway with a flute case and a granola bar, took one look at their faces, and said, "What did you two break?"

"Nothing. Tristan found something." Aryan sounded almost proud, which Tristan found suspicious, since Aryan usually reserved pride for himself. "Compare the two spots. The second theme returns in the home key instead of the dominant. That's why the ending feels like arriving instead of like more traveling."

Jacey set down her case and looked over Aryan's shoulder. "So when we played this in ensemble last year and the ending felt like it landed, that was why? It wasn't just that we finally played something in tune?"

"It was never that you played something in tune," Aryan said, and she hit him with the granola bar.

Tristan marked the two bars in the score, then wrote in the margin, small, so no one could read it over his shoulder: second theme, home key here. He had spent the whole week thinking the assignment was about finding boundaries, drawing lines between sections, and the lines had kept refusing to hold still. Now he thought it might be about hearing the same thing twice and admitting it had changed, and he wasn't sure whether that was a real insight or just the kind of thing you think at ten o'clock, so he decided, in his usual way, that he believed it tonight and would check whether he still believed it in the morning.

Ms. Sultani came in to unlock the cabinet for the metronomes, saw the score, and paused. "You've marked the double return."

"The what?"

"The first theme and the second, both coming back." She tapped the second theme in the recapitulation without further comment, which was her way, and Tristan found he liked her better for it, since he'd half expected her to explain everything and take the finding away from him.

"You found it yourself?" Jacey asked.

"Mostly," he said, which was the most honest word available, since Aryan had held the score and Ms. Sultani had tapped the bar and the whole thing had happened in the space between three people, like some mutualism where you couldn't say who had contributed what. Or maybe that was another ten o'clock thought. He put the pencil in his pocket.

Aryan began tightening his bow. "Play it," he said. "Both places. I want to hear the key change, not just look at it."

Tristan set his hands on the keys, played the second theme once in the dominant, where it wandered, and then again in the home key, where it arrived, and outside the window the parking lot lights came on.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: China's campaign to kill sparrows, launched in 1958, removed a predator of crop-eating insects, and locust swarms that followed contributed to the Great Chinese Famine.
story:
The seminar room smelled like the radiator's dusty breath, and Avery had positioned herself near the window because the community garden was visible from there, four raised beds behind the science wing, half of their seed rows already pecked bare. Ms. Dela Cruz had posted the problem on the board that morning: the garden committee wanted a vote on netting the beds and driving off the sparrows for good. Kaylee had collected sixty signatures in favor. Jensen had drawn a sparrow on the petition's margin, which everyone agreed was unhelpful.

"Sparrows are pests," Kaylee said, sliding the petition across the seminar table. "They eat the seeds before the seeds become anything. We planted two hundred bean seeds and got eleven plants. Eleven. My little brother could count them."

Jensen turned his pen over in his fingers. "They're birds, though. It's not like they're doing it out of spite."

"They're doing it out of hunger, which is worse, because hunger doesn't negotiate."

Avery looked out at the beds again. She had signed the petition on Tuesday, in the hallway, without thinking, the way she signed most things Kaylee put in front of her. Since then the signature had been sitting somewhere behind her sternum like an unpaid debt. She wanted to expiate it somehow, though she hadn't yet worked out what that would look like, since one couldn't unsign a petition the way one untagged a photo.

Ms. Dela Cruz, who ran the seminar as a referee rather than a lecturer, said only, "Before we vote, does anyone have evidence? Not feelings. Evidence." She wrote the word on the board and underlined it once, which for her was theatrical.

Avery's mind had been drifting, and the word evidence landed on her mid-reverie and scattered it. The thing was, she did have something. Last spring, before finals, she had watched a documentary at her grandmother's apartment while rain ran down the windows, one of those slow archival films her grandmother liked. There had been a segment about China, about a campaign launched in 1958 to kill sparrows, citizens banging pots until the birds fell from the sky out of exhaustion. She had half-watched it, half-worked a calculus problem, but one detail had stuck to her the way burrs stick to socks: the sparrows had been predators of crop-eating insects. With the birds gone, locust swarms followed, and those swarms contributed to the Great Chinese Famine. She remembered sitting up on her grandmother's couch and saying, "Wait, they killed the birds to protect the crops?" and her grandmother saying, "That's usually how it goes," and going back to her crossword.

"Evidence," Avery said now, and her voice came out lower than she intended. "In 1958, China ran a campaign to kill sparrows. Whole country. People thought the sparrows were eating their grain." Kaylee's eyebrows went up in a way that meant and. "But sparrows also eat insects. They're a predator of crop-eating insects. Take away the predator, and the insects do whatever they want. Locust swarms came after. And the locusts contributed to the famine." She heard herself say famine and watched the room get quieter, the way a bus gets quieter when someone drops a phone.

"Okay," Kaylee said slowly, "but we're not causing a famine. We're protecting eleven hypothetical bean plants."

"We're removing a predator," Avery said. "That's the same action at a different size." She paused, because she could hear the equivocal shape of her own argument, the way it could be read as principle or as melodrama, and she genuinely didn't know which it was. "Maybe. I don't actually know what our sparrows eat besides our seeds. I'm not pretending I ran a study."

Ms. Dela Cruz was writing nothing on the board, which meant she was listening. "So what's the proposal, Avery?"

"Net the beds," Avery said. "Netting keeps the seeds in and the birds alive. We don't have to decide the birds are the problem. We just make it inconvenient for them for six weeks." She looked at Kaylee. "You can still be furious about the beans."

"I'm going to be furious about the beans either way," Kaylee said, but she was looking at the garden through the window now, at the bare rows and the fence and the one sparrow sitting on the hose reel like a small brown comma. "Netting costs money, though. The committee has forty dollars and a roll of chicken wire."

Jensen raised his pen like a gavel. "Motion to spend the forty dollars on bird netting and to amend the petition to say, in small letters, that we're sorry."

"Nobody reads the small letters," Kaylee said.

"I read the small letters," said Jensen, and passed the petition down the table for signatures again, Avery's old one still sitting near the top, next to the sparrow he'd drawn with its beak open, mid-song.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Galileo showed that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola, in his book Two New Sciences, published in 1638.
story:
Joseph arrived at the skate park with his physics worksheet folded into quarters in his back pocket, because Mr. Goh had said the retake was Monday and Joseph had gotten a forty-two on the original, and his father had said nothing at all about the forty-two, which was worse than shouting. Hugo was already there, waxing the coping on the quarter pipe, and Matthew sat on the flat bottom with his phone balanced on his knee, half watching Hugo and half reading something about first-year courses.

"You're studying on a Saturday," Matthew said, not looking up. "At a skate park. That's a new depth."

"I'm studying here because I don't understand it anywhere," Joseph said. He unfolded the worksheet on the concrete. The problem showed a ball launched at some angle with some speed, and asked where it would land, and every time Joseph tried to combine the numbers they collapsed into nothing he recognized. "Mr. Goh keeps saying treat the horizontal and vertical separately, like that's supposed to mean something. But it's one ball. It goes one way."

Hugo dropped in, carved up the opposite wall, and came back down without doing anything fancy, just carrying speed through the bowl. He rolled to a stop near them, one foot on the board. "One ball," he said. "Two questions. How far, and how high. That's how I think about a kickflip. Out and up. If I think about them together I land on my face."

"That's not physics," Joseph said.

"Everything is physics," Hugo said, and pushed off again.

Joseph watched him this time instead of the worksheet. Hugo approached the hip at an angle, popped the board, and for the fraction of a second he was airborne Joseph could see the thing Mr. Goh had been describing: Hugo rose and fell, quick and even in a way Joseph suddenly recognized, while at the same time drifting sideways across the bowl, smooth and unhurried, as if some part of him had never left the ground. Two motions in one body. The up part slowed, stopped, came back down. The across part just kept going. They had nothing to do with each other. He looked at the worksheet and, for the first time, at the little grid beneath the problem, the axes Mr. Goh had printed faintly for them to sketch on.

He took out his pencil and separated the launch speed into a piece that pointed up and a piece that pointed sideways, the way Hugo's body had separated itself in the air. He worked the vertical numbers the way he would work a ball thrown straight up, and he worked the horizontal numbers as plain distance equals rate times time, and where the two calculations shared a variable, the time, he stitched them together. The ball landed. He checked the back of the sheet, where the answer was printed upside down, and it matched. He sat very still, the way you do when something that was arithmetic a minute ago is suddenly the world.

"It's a parabola," he said. "If you plot the height against the distance, the path is a parabola. Galileo showed that, ignoring air resistance. It's in his book, Two New Sciences, 1638."

Matthew looked up properly now. "How do you know that?"

"Read it Tuesday night instead of doing the worksheet," Joseph admitted. "Which is arguably why I got the forty-two." He grinned, then stopped grinning. "I knew the sentence but I didn't know what it meant. Now the graph means it."

Matthew held up his phone, and on it was a photo from the open-day visit to the science museum, the curved jet of the drinking fountain frozen mid-arc, which he had apparently taken for reasons of his own, some folder of pictures of things that looked like other things. The jet made the same shape as the graph. Neither of them said anything for a second.

The three of them were going different directions in the autumn, and they all knew it; Matthew had spent the morning reading about immunology, because the medical programmes wanted evidence of interest, and Hugo had a sponsor who talked about competitions in the city, and Joseph had nothing decided except the retake. Matthew had made some trenchant remark about this last week, that Joseph treated every decision as a problem with a printed answer on the back, and Joseph had not spoken to him for two days. Now, looking at the fountain and the graph and Hugo carving the bowl, Joseph found he had to adjudicate between two ideas of himself: the one who wanted every problem to have a printed answer, and the one who had just watched a boy on a skateboard split into two independent motions and seen it work. He could not fully reconcile them. Air resistance was real, for one thing; the parabola was true only if you ignored it, and the world did not ignore it. He wrote at the bottom of the sheet, in small letters, "ignoring air," and left it there.

"Throw me the marker," Hugo called from the top of the bowl, meaning the one they used to scuff lines on the coping, and Joseph tossed it, a little high and a little wide on purpose, so that it arced.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Paul Graham's 2008 essay 'How to Disagree' ranks disagreement in seven levels, from name-calling at the bottom to refuting the other person's central point at the top.
story:
James opened the email from Mr. Kamau on the library computer before first period, because the subject line read "Re: Re: Re: Volunteer Saturday," and a thread that long never meant anything good. The message said only: "James, the group-chat transcript you forwarded was concerning. Come by after last bell. Bring your thoughts, not your defenses."

The transcript had come from the night before. Ryley wanted the volunteer day moved to the river cleanup, Baby wanted the food bank, and by eleven o'clock the argument had stopped being about either. Somebody had typed that Ryley couldn't read a map, somebody had typed something worse about Baby, and James had sat in his dark bedroom watching the screen, thumbs hovering, typing "guys" four times and deleting it four times. Then he had screenshotted the whole slide and sent it to Mr. Kamau with the subject line "is there a way to fix this," which now, in the morning light, felt like a tattletale's move.

At three-fifteen he found Mr. Kamau grading in the emptying science lab. "Sit," his teacher said, not unkindly, and James sat, backpack on his knees like a shield.

"I didn't send it to get anyone in trouble," James said.

"I know. But you sent it to me instead of to them." Mr. Kamau turned the laptop so James could see the thread again. "Read me what you would have said. Out loud, the way you'd want it to sound in writing."

James read his drafts, the ones with the deleted "guys." Each one came out as a plea, or worse, as a shrug. "Nothing I say lands," he finished. "It just becomes another message they scroll past."

"So don't scroll past this," Mr. Kamau said, and wrote a single name on a sticky note and slid it across the desk. "Paul Graham. Look him up tonight. Then write to the group the way you'd write to a college, not the way you'd write to a wall." He did not say anything further about it, only stacked his papers and added, "And when you write to me next, give me a subject line that tells me what the email is about."

That night, at his desk with the door shut, James searched the name. He found an essay called "How to Disagree," published in 2008, and read it twice with a pencil in his hand. On a napkin he copied out the shape of it. "Seven levels," he said under his breath, drawing a ladder. At the bottom of the ladder he wrote name-calling, because that was where the group chat had been living all week. At the top he wrote refuting the central point, and he looked at those two rungs for a long time. His room felt briefly like an interregnum, the old order of the chat dead and no new one yet installed, and he was the only one who seemed to notice the throne was empty.

He opened his email, not the chat, because Mr. Kamau had said college, not wall, and because an email could not be interrupted mid-sentence by three people typing insults. He began three times. His first draft called Ryley impatient and Baby stubborn, and he deleted it, recognizing too late that he was doing the bottom rung with better spelling. His second draft tried to be so polite it said nothing at all. The third draft took forty minutes and two outlines on the napkin, and it read, in part: "The disagreement here is not about who is rude. It is about whether our group's Saturday does more good at the river cleanup or the food bank. Ryley's central point is that the cleanup is understaffed this month. Baby's central point is that the food bank serves more people per hour of labor. Both of these can be checked. I propose we check them by Thursday and decide on evidence. I was wrong to stay silent while the argument slid sideways. That silence was my own low rung."

He sent it to the group and then, after a minute, forwarded it to Mr. Kamau with the subject line "Group plan for Saturday, decision by Thursday." The reply came in eleven minutes: "Now that is an email. One question. Which rung are they at when they answer you?"

The answer arrived by morning, and it was split. Baby wrote back a full paragraph, half apology, half argument about food bank logistics, and cited a number from the pantry's website. Ryley wrote back a thumbs-up and a link to the watershed council's signup sheet, which Ryley apparently took as a complete rebuttal. But the insults had stopped, and a nascent thread formed, short and businesslike, assigning who would call which coordinator. It was not warm. It was, for the first time in a week, about something.

On Saturday James stood between them at the food bank loading dock, because the evidence had favored Baby by a margin nobody liked to gloat about, and Ryley had come anyway, stacking cans with a deliberate, recuperative slowness, as if the work itself could patch what Tuesday had torn. Between cartloads Ryley said, without looking up, "Your email was still kind of a move."

"Which part?"

"The outline part. Like a teacher wrote it."

James handed Ryley another flat of soup and said, "A teacher sort of did."

Ryley laughed once, surprised, then set the cans down carefully, in rows.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five 'filters', the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations.
story:
The printer in the student newspaper office jammed at 7:40 on Tuesday night, twenty minutes before the issue had to go to the district print shop, and Charles knelt on the floor coaxing the paper tray loose while Carolyn read headlines over his shoulder. The lead story was his, eight hundred words on the school board's decision to hand the district's stadium naming rights to Veltrix Energy, the company whose logo already hung above the gym scoreboard and whose regional vice president, according to the district's own donor list, had written two cheques to the superintendent's re-election fund.

"Ledgerlin owns the County Courier too," Carolyn said. She had her laptop open to the Courier's website, where the stadium deal was described in the ninth paragraph of a story about "district modernization," beneath an ad for Veltrix's residential solar packages. "Ledgerlin Media. I looked it up."

Charles got the tray free and stood, wiping toner from his palms onto his jeans. He had read Manufacturing Consent over the weekend for Ms. Farah-Ali's seminar, Herman and Chomsky's 1988 book, and it had argued that news is shaped by five filters, the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations. He'd underlined so much of the first chapter that the page had gone grey at the margins, and then he had done the thing the book seemed to invite, which was to start noticing who owned everything he read. The Courier's parent company. The two radio stations. The regional chain that had bought the alternative weekly and quietly retired its investigations desk.

"So the Courier isn't lying," he said. "It's just putting the deal in paragraph nine and the solar ad above it."

"Which is worse, kind of," said Amelie from the layout desk, where she was collating the proof pages into order, squaring the corners with a slap of her hand. "A lie you can catch."

Ms. Farah-Ali, who advised the paper and had a standing habit of appearing at deadline only to eat whatever food the staff had abandoned, leaned in the doorway with a container of cold noodles. "How's the Veltrix piece holding up?"

"Fine," Charles said. "Except the angle changed."

The deadline was real: the print shop closed at eight-thirty, and if the file didn't reach them by then, the paper came out Thursday instead of Wednesday, which meant it hit the hallways a day after the school board's public forum on the deal, which meant his story would be covering a question the community had already stopped asking. He'd learned that arithmetic last spring, during the parking-lot paving scandal, when a late issue had run his story two days after the board voted and his father had said, not unkindly, "That's not news, that's an obituary."

He sat down at his laptop and looked at the paragraph he'd written at five o'clock, the one that said "some observers question the timing of the sponsorship." It was a paragraph built to survive, vague enough to offend no one, and he understood now that it was a paragraph nine of his own, a little filter he'd installed without being asked. Veltrix didn't own this paper. Nobody owned this paper. But the principal had to sign off on every issue, and the principal answered to the board, and the board was about to accept a cheque, and somewhere in the back of his mind Charles had already done that math and sanded his sentences down accordingly.

"I want to add who owns the Courier," he said. "And that Ledgerlin took sponsorship money from Veltrix last year, for the county fair. It's in their own archives."

Amelie stopped squaring pages. "We'll never make eight-thirty."

"We'll make it if I cut the history of stadium naming, which nobody reads, and put the ownership in paragraph three."

Carolyn turned her laptop so he could see the corporate registry page, the nested names like boxes inside boxes. "Herman and Chomsky," she said, testing the names. "Your seminar book. You made it sound like a conspiracy theory on Friday."

"It's not a conspiracy," Charles said. "That's what I got wrong. It's a filter. Nobody at the Courier got a memo. The structure does it." He was typing as he talked, replacing his safe paragraph with something plainer: the district's most-read news source is owned by a company that does business with the stadium's sponsor. He read the sentence back and felt the strange, incipient freedom of saying a thing that was simply checkable. In economics the year before, they had studied stagflation, prices rising while the economy stalled, and his teacher had called it a word for a condition people insisted couldn't exist until it did. This felt related, naming a thing people said wasn't happening.

"Seven minutes," Amelie said.

He trimmed the cutline, fixed a transposed number in the sponsorship figure, and sent the file. The progress bar crawled. Ms. Farah-Ali ate her noodles. When the confirmation came back, the room made the small noise rooms make when a deadline passes without disaster, half exhale, half laugh.

"There's one thing I can't tell," Charles admitted, saving the backup. "Whether paragraph three changes anything, or whether people just read the headline and the sports scores."

"Then you print it and find out," Ms. Farah-Ali said. She dropped her empty container in the bin and picked up her coat. "Wednesday's a data point."

Amelie stacked the proofs and slid them into her bag, and Carolyn closed the registry page with its nested boxes, and Charles looked at the printer, still warm, its green light steady. Tomorrow he would stand in the hallway and watch people pick the paper up, or not pick it up, and count.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The line at the community hall moved slowly, which surprised Nicholas, because he had expected voting to be fast, a machine you stepped into and out of. Instead there were folding tables and a smell of burnt coffee and an elderly woman ahead of him arguing gently with a poll worker about whether her registration card had expired. He had turned eighteen nine days ago, and the card in his hand still felt like something issued to someone older.

His phone buzzed. A message from his mother, who was on shift at the hospital and could not come: "Your grandfather voted for the first time in 1972. He says to tell you the age was lowered from 21 to 18 only two years before that, in 1970, so he barely made it in himself. He was angry about it for years, that he'd missed the earlier elections. He says vote however you want, but vote like someone who almost couldn't." Nicholas read it twice. He had never heard his grandfather describe himself as almost anything.

Behind him, Byron was reading over his shoulder, which Byron did without asking, the way he had since grade four. "Lowered in 1970," Byron said. "So people our age have only been allowed since then. Fifty-odd years." He said it the way he said things in debate club, testing the weight of a fact before deciding what to do with it.

"Allowed," Nicholas repeated. The word had a shape he didn't like, though he couldn't delimit exactly why, where the permission ended and the entitlement began.

"Fine, entitled," Byron said. "Same thing."

It wasn't the same thing, and Nicholas knew that the distinction mattered more than either of them could articulate in a church basement line. He thought of Mr. Kelly, his civics teacher, who had refused all year to tell the class how he voted, saying only that a vote was the one opinion you were obligated to form alone. Nicholas had found that infuriating in October and useful now.

The elderly woman resolved her problem with the registration card and shuffled toward the booth. The poll worker, a man with an auxiliary badge pinned under his name tag, someone there to help but not to decide anything, waved Nicholas forward. "First time?" the man asked, and when Nicholas nodded, he said, "You'll have to sign the box, that's all. The rest is yours."

Byron leaned in before Nicholas stepped up. "You're still going Liberal? You said your dad." Byron's own father had put a sign on their lawn, and Byron had defended it at lunch with Lyam for two weeks straight, not convincingly, but loudly.

"That was my dad's argument," Nicholas said. "He treated it like a family phylum, like you inherit it down the line." It had come out harsher than he meant. He lowered his voice. "My grandfather's message, though. He's voted everything, all over, his whole life. He said vote like someone who almost couldn't. That's not a direction. That's a way of doing it."

Byron looked at him without the debate-club face. "So you don't know."

"I know it matters," Nicholas said. "I know I read all the platforms, even the boring pages about the auxiliary funding for the transit thing. I know my dad's mad about the mill and my mom's mad about the hospital cuts and my grandfather thinks it's a miracle any of us get a say." He realized he was holding the registration card too tightly, creasing it. "Two of those are probably right. I don't know which two."

The poll worker coughed, politely. The line behind Byron had grown; Lyam was visible near the back, headphones in, holding his own card like a hall pass he intended to forge ahead with regardless.

Nicholas stepped to the table and signed the box. The pen was chained. The booth, when he pulled the curtain, was smaller than a confessional and lit by one bulb, and the ballot paper lay there with its circles, the whole ridiculous and enormous mechanism of it reduced to graphite marks. His grandfather had been twenty in 1970 when the age came down from 21, twenty when the country decided he counted, and had never once skipped an election since. Nicholas stood in the booth with the pencil hovering.

From outside the curtain, Byron's voice, low: "Take your time. It's yours."

Nicholas marked the first circle, then stopped, and looked at it for a long moment, eraser already in his other hand.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
story:
I already knew what the fine print said before I read it, which is how I like to do things, and it's also, Musa tells me, why I'm impossible. I was at the front desk of the Northgate gym on the first Tuesday of the summer holidays, holding a pen that someone had chewed, reading the membership terms upside down while Ms. Banerjee sorted a stack of day passes behind the counter. She had this dour way of greeting people that I'd stopped taking personally years ago, back when she was just the neighbour who complained about our bins. Now she was the only adult standing between me and the weight room, and the clipboard between us was doing most of the talking.

"Liability waiver, code of conduct, photo consent," she said, tapping three places on the form. "Initial each box. Signature at the bottom, and your parent's beside it, since you're under eighteen."

That was the part I'd been dreading, not because my mother would refuse but because she'd want to read every line out loud at the kitchen table first, and the summer was short. I read the liability paragraph myself instead. It said the gym wasn't responsible for injury except where the law didn't allow them to dodge it, which struck me as a strange thing to admit in your own contract, like a confession with an escape hatch. I initialled the boxes. My pen hovered over the signature line, because a signature felt different from initials, heavier, a whole self instead of fragments of one.

That was when Musa came through the glass doors with his bike helmet still on, which is how I knew it was serious. He never wears the helmet unless he's riding, and he wasn't riding.

"I sold the bike," he said, before I could ask. "This morning. That bloke from the allotments, the one with the trailer. Twenty quid."

The bike was worth three hundred. Everyone knew that; Musa had rebuilt the gears himself in his dad's garage over Easter, and Lilianne had photographed it for the school leavers' raffle before it got pulled from the list. I said, "Twenty quid for the Cannondale," and he said, "He had cash right there," and his voice had gone flat in the way it does when he's already rehearsed the story a dozen times on the ride over and it hasn't improved with rehearsal.

"He knocked on the door while I was cleaning it. Said his grandson needed a bike. I felt bad saying a big number to a grandfather."

"You felt bad," I said. "So you gave him a two-hundred-and-eighty-pound discount." I was aware of Ms. Banerjee listening, and I was aware, less comfortably, of a conversation three months ago in which Musa had given me half his bus fare for no reason and I'd said nothing, which had desensitized me a little to his generosity, made it seem like a law of nature rather than a choice he kept making. That's my defence, anyway. I've told the story other ways.

"I'll text him," Musa said. "I'll say it was a mistake. There's got to be a rule that a deal that bad doesn't count. There's got to be." He looked at me like I'd know, because I'm the person who reads forms before signing them, or at least the person who claims to, and the gap between those two people is wider than anyone at school suspects.

I picked up my phone, mostly to have something to do with my hands. I typed can you cancel a sale if price too low, then deleted it because it sounded like something a child would ask, then typed it again because it was the truth. What came up was a page about contracts, dense with words I only half knew, but one line surfaced out of the stratum of legal text like a coin at the bottom of a birdbath. I read it twice, then out loud, slowly, because I didn't believe it the first time.

"Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price." Musa stared at me. "It says courts don't generally judge whether a bargain was a good one."

"Consideration," he repeated.

"The thing you get back. The twenty quid. It has to be worth something, but it doesn't have to be fair." I turned the phone toward him. The words sat there being the words they were. Ms. Banerjee had stopped sorting day passes and was watching us over her glasses, and she didn't say anything, which I think was deliberate, the way a good coach steps back at the exact moment you need to find your own footing.

"So it counts," Musa said. "Twenty quid counts."

"It counts. You can't undo it just because it was terrible." I wanted to find him a loophole the way I always find loopholes, in timetables and curfews and the seating plan for the leavers' meal, but the page was plain about that too. A bad bargain was still a bargain. Unless there was something else, duress or fraud or mistake, and the bloke from the allotments hadn't done anything except stand on a doorstep with cash and a story about a grandson, and Musa hadn't done anything except be Musa.

"He'll probably say no," I said. "If you text."

"I know." He unbuckled the helmet and held it under his arm. "But maybe his grandson doesn't even exist. Maybe I ask, and if the grandson exists, then fine, it's the grandson's bike now, and if he made him up, I'll know something." He pulled out his phone and started typing, standing right there next to the desk with his thumbs going fast, while I still had the pen in my hand and no signature on the line.

Ms. Banerjee slid the clipboard half an inch closer to me. "You can take it home," she said. "Or you can sign it now and start today."

I read the last paragraph again, the one about consent to photos for the gym's social media, and I wrote my initials in the third box. Then, in the signature line, I wrote my full name, all three words of it, more carefully than I had since primary school. Across the desk Musa's phone buzzed once in his hand.

"Message from him," he said, and didn't look up.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
The morning of the funeral, Tyler sat in the back seat of the family car with his grandfather's harmonica in his coat pocket, and he had not decided yet whether he was going to play it at the cemetery or not. His mother drove. Jakob rode beside him because Jakob's own parents were working and Tyler had offered two days ago, back when the offer had felt simple.

Traffic on the overpass was stopped, so there was time to think, which was the problem. Two nights ago Tyler had found the harmonica while cleaning out his grandfather's dresser, and every night since he had taken it out before sleeping and said something to the ceiling. Small things. A score from a game. The fact that he had passed his road test. He had started to wonder whether he was losing it a little.

"You're doing the thing with your thumb," Jakob said. "The fretting thing."

"Sorry." Tyler flattened his hand.

"It's fine. You can talk, you know. Or not."

Tyler pulled out his phone, opened the screenshot he had saved, and passed it over. It was a page from a psychology reader, an excerpt his class had been assigned in the spring, from a book called Continuing Bonds, published in 1996, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman. He had skimmed it at the time for the quiz. Then, at one in the morning with the harmonica warm in his hand, he had gone back and read the whole thing twice. The argument, as far as he could hold it, was that keeping a lasting connection with someone who died was a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.

"I talked to him," Tyler said. "Last night. To the harmonica, kind of. Is that insane?"

Jakob read for a while, tilting the screen against the window light. "It's in a book," he said finally. "People wrote a whole book about it. It can't be that insane."

"That's what I'm saying. But I don't know if a book makes it okay or just makes it a documented kind of crazy."

His mother signalled and changed lanes, and the cemetery gate came up faster than Tyler expected, iron posts and a hedge trimmed flat. In the parking lot the cars were already lined up, his uncle's truck, the neighbour's little sedan, and somewhere a cousin's toddler was being obstreperous about getting out of a car seat, the crying carrying across the rows. His mother turned around. "Ten minutes, then we go in. Do you want to say something during the service? You don't have to."

"I might," Tyler said. "Not words. Something else."

After the service, which was short and mostly psalms, the family stood around the grave while the pastor finished, and the wind moved the hedge the way his grandfather's breath used to move the reeds inside the harmonica when he warmed it up. Tyler had watched him do it a hundred times on the porch, blowing a low note first, always the same low note, before anything else. There was no recompense for any of it, his grandfather had said once about a different loss entirely, no payment that squared things up; you just kept the instrument and kept playing. Tyler had not understood that at fourteen. He thought he understood some of it now, though not all, and he was honest enough with himself to know the difference between those two.

He took the harmonica out. The cousins had gone quiet; even the toddler had been distracted with a biscuit. Jakob stood a step behind him, and when Tyler glanced back, Jakob gave him a small nod, as if to say the gesture would instantiate the whole idea better than any speech: the connection kept, deliberately, in front of everyone.

Tyler played the low note. It came out clean, and then it wavered, and he let it waver. "That one's yours," he said quietly, to no one visible, and put the harmonica back in his pocket as his mother reached for his arm and the family began walking toward the cars.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Sea ice reflects most sunlight while open ocean absorbs most of it, so melting ice exposes darker water that warms and melts more ice: a reinforcing feedback loop.
story:
Morgan had signed up for environmental science because the course catalog made it sound easy, a semester of diagrams and vocabulary, and now Mr. Perera was handing back the proposal drafts with the mine map clipped to hers. The town council meeting was in nine days, and her class had been assigned to present on the quarry expansion behind the high school, the one that would cut into the riparian corridor along the creek and add forty trucks a day to the road past the elementary school.

"They liked your draft," Mr. Perera said, tapping her paper. "Except the part where you treat economics and ecology as separate columns. The council will not experience them as separate columns."

She took her seat between Renee and Genesis. Renee's father drove one of the trucks already, and Renee had spent all of last week arguing at lunch that forty more meant steady overtime, meant her family could stop choosing between the dentist and the car insurance. Genesis had grown up two streets from the creek and kept a photo on her phone of the heron colony that would sit directly in the blast zone. Morgan had written her first draft standing in the middle, which was another way of saying she had written nothing at all.

That afternoon Mr. Perera put a satellite image of the Arctic on the board and asked them what they noticed. Nobody answered, so he drew an arrow, then another, and left the room to fetch a stack of handouts, which was his way of making them do the work. Genesis leaned forward. "Okay, so the ice is white," she said slowly. "White stuff reflects. So if it melts..."

"Then it's ocean instead," Morgan said, and something assembled itself in her head with an almost audible click. "Open ocean is dark. Dark absorbs." She took the marker from the ledge and sketched it: bright ice throwing sunlight back, dark water drinking it in, the warmed water melting the ice at its edges, new dark water absorbing more, melting more. "It doesn't just warm up. It warms up and then warms itself up faster."

"It's called a reinforcing feedback loop," Mr. Perera said from the doorway, setting down the handouts, and moved on to attendance.

Morgan sat with the shape of it through the rest of class and all through the walk home. Not the Arctic, exactly. She was thinking about the quarry. Renee's family needed the money; the money depended on the trucks; the trucks degraded the creek; a degraded creek meant worse flooding in Genesis's neighborhood, which was the neighborhood with the least money to fix it, which pushed people like Renee's family harder toward the next job that made things worse. Each turn fed the next turn. She could not prove that with a marker, but she could not unsee it either, and she remembered, unhappily, that last spring she had laughed along when a boy in her history class called the creek people "the flood lottery people." She had let that comment ionize the room, had felt the joke spread and attach itself to houses and families, and she had said nothing. That was a loop too, she thought, though a smaller and more human one.

The next day she found Renee at her locker before first period. "I'm not going to stand up there and pretend the jobs don't matter," Morgan said. "But I can't pretend the creek doesn't either. I want to put both in the presentation. Your dad's numbers and the herons and the flooding, all of it, as one system."

Renee shut her locker and looked at her for a long moment. "If you make my dad the villain in front of the whole council, I will never speak to you again."

"That's not what a system means," Morgan said. "Nobody in it is the villain. That's kind of the point. Or the problem. I honestly can't tell which."

For three evenings the three of them worked in Genesis's kitchen, arguing over phrasing, eating her mother's rice, crossing out more than they kept. Renee brought the wage figures and the attrition rate at the plant, the way drivers quit when the routes got cut, and she read those numbers aloud without apologizing for them. Genesis brought the flood maps. Morgan drew the arrows. Some of them she drew in pencil, because she was not certain the connections held, and she left them pencil in the final slides, which Mr. Perera noticed and did not correct.

The night before the council meeting she stood in her driveway in the cold, looking at the one bright patch of sky between the streetlights, trying to rehearse her opening line and hearing instead her own voice saying it doesn't just warm up, it warms itself up faster. She did not know yet whether the council would listen or whether listening would change anything. She only knew she had stopped standing in the middle, because the middle, it turned out, was not a place at all. She pulled the slides up on her phone one more time and pressed play on the practice run.

"Genesis, hit the lights," she said. "Start the timer."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Migration can reshape a pyramid: some Gulf states, such as Qatar, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there.
story:
The airport in Doha sat between flights like a held breath, and Samuel spread his project folder on the bench beside gate B14 while Lea went to buy water. Their connecting flight to Kathmandu left in three hours. Their geography project, due by email at midnight, had to be finished before they slept.

He had chosen Qatar almost at random, a country whose pyramid he assumed would be simple. It wasn't. The chart showed a shape he'd never seen in class: narrow at the very bottom, then a slab of population stacked between twenty and fifty, and the slab itself lopsided, the male bars stretching far past the female ones on the other side of the centre line. He counted the bars twice, then turned his laptop toward Joe, who was slouched two seats down with his headphones around his neck.

"It's wrong," Samuel said. "The data's corrupted or something. A population can't look like this."

Joe leaned over, nonchalant at first, then less so. "That's a lot of dudes."

"That's the point. There's no country of mostly men aged thirty. So the source is bad, and if the source is bad the whole project's bad." His voice came out sharper than he meant. He'd been the one who told Ms. Zhao, back in October, that he could handle the demographic futures unit alone. He could still see her tapping the rubric with one finger, saying, "Prediction is the hard part, Samuel. Anyone can read a chart."

Lea came back with two bottles and sat down. She looked at the screen for maybe ten seconds, chewing the cap of her pen. "Wait," she said. "Remember the video with the Dubai construction sites? Everyone working on that tower was from somewhere else. Nepal, Bangladesh, the Philippines."

"So?"

"So maybe they get counted. If all those workers are men, and they're living there, maybe the pyramid isn't wrong. Maybe it's just not showing births. It's showing who's in the country."

Samuel's first instinct was to argue, because the project was his and the mistake, if it was a mistake, was his too. Instead he opened a second browser tab and typed the question plainly. The results loaded over the airport's slow wifi, one paragraph at a time, and there it was: he wasn't looking at an error. Migration could reshape a pyramid like that. Some Gulf states, such as Qatar, showed a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers lived there. He read it twice, then a third time, feeling the ground shift under an assumption he hadn't known he was standing on.

"It's real," he said. "The chart's real."

Lea pulled the laptop closer. "Then your prediction has to change, right? You wrote that they'd need nursing homes."

He had. His draft argued that a narrow base meant a greying population, that schools would atrophy while eldercare expanded, and he'd been proud of the sentence. Now he stared at the male bulge and tried to fold it in. A country full of working-age men, most of whom presumably intended to leave someday, or whose families lived elsewhere. Did they need schools? Did they need nursing homes? Or did they need neither, because the pyramid described a population that was passing through rather than aging in place?

"You can't tell from the shape alone," he said slowly. "You have to know whether the people in the bars are staying."

"That's not on the rubric," Joe said, not unkindly.

"Then the rubric's wrong too." Samuel opened his draft and, in the gate area of an airport halfway across the world, deleted three paragraphs and began again. He wrote that a pyramid was evidence but not a verdict; that the same chart could mean schools in one country and neither schools nor nursing homes in another; that Qatar's bulge of foreign male workers made any long-range prediction honest only if it admitted what it couldn't know. He kept one old sentence, the one about hedonism, arguing that a young transient population built cities for pleasure rather than for generations, though even that, he now suspected, was a guess dressed up as a conclusion.

Somewhere over his shoulder the departure board flipped to Kathmandu, FINAL CALL, though their gate hadn't opened yet. Lea closed his laptop over his hands, gently, the way you close a book on someone still reading.

"You can finish on the plane," she said. "Or you can leave it like that, with the question at the end."

Samuel looked at the shut lid, then at the board, then at the queue already forming. He picked up the laptop and slung his pack over one shoulder, and Lea asked which one he'd decided, and he didn't answer until they were at the back of the line, and then all he said was, "Ask me when we land."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, passed over President Truman's veto, allowed US states to pass right-to-work laws banning contracts that require workers to pay union fees.
story:
The kitchen of the Marigold Grill went quiet only in the lull between the lunch rush and the dinner prep, and that was when Chase, sixteen and three weeks into his first real job, liked to stand at the sink and let the steam unclench his shoulders. He had taken the job for the money, plainly enough, saving toward a car that existed so far only as a photograph on his phone. But the kitchen had turned out to be more than wages. It was a place where people argued about wages, out loud, while chopping onions.

The argument that afternoon was between Romeo, who had moved from Michigan in the spring, and Dax, who had arrived from Georgia in August. Romeo wiped his hands and said that everyone on staff paid union dues here, that it was in the contract, that the union was why they got overtime after forty hours and why the walk-in freezer had actually been fixed. Dax said he had never paid dues in his life and wasn't about to start. "Back home nobody made me," he said. "There's a name for that kind of state. Right-to-work."

Chase kept his hands in the suds and listened.
