He understood, in a vague way, that the union bargained for all of them, that there was a contract posted by the time clock with a number for the wage scale and a paragraph about breaks. What he did not understand was how Dax could simply refuse. He had assumed rules were rules, the same everywhere. Romeo said the rules were different depending on the state, and Dax said Romeo was wrong, and the two of them looked at Chase as though he might be a tiebreaker.

"I don't know," Chase admitted. "I don't know anything about it." He said it without embarrassment, because it was true, and because saying true things out loud was a habit he was trying to build before college, where he assumed everyone would know everything. Ms. Asante, the shift supervisor, passed through for the produce order and said only, "Look it up yourself, Chase. Don't take anybody's word in an argument like that." She said it kindly and kept walking, carrying a crate of peppers.

At his break, I sat in the alley behind the kitchen with my phone and my half of a stolen roll, and I searched. It took me four tries to get the words in the right order, and then the history assembled itself: the Taft-Hartley Act, passed in 1947 over President Truman's veto, which allowed states to pass right-to-work laws, banning contracts that required workers to pay union fees. Michigan had never passed such a law, or had passed and repealed it; Georgia had one. So Romeo and Dax were both telling the truth about their own lives. Neither was lying, and both were certain. I read the sentence twice more, trying to interpolate what it would mean for me, standing at the sink, if I ever had to choose whether to pay.

When I came back inside, the argument had calcified into silence. Romeo scrubbed the flat top with the fury of a man scrubbing an idea. Dax stacked to-go boxes with exaggerated calm. The shift had lost its usual rhythm, the way a room does when two people are not speaking. I told them what I had found, carefully, without taking a side, and watched Dax's shoulders come down an inch. "So it's legal either way," he said. "Here too. I can work here and not pay."

"That's what it says," I said. Romeo turned around, sponge dripping. "But the union still covers you," he said. "You get the wage either way. That's the part that gets me." It was the first thing either of them had said all afternoon that wasn't a restatement of a position, and it landed on me harder than the rest. Somewhere between the statute and the sink, a question opened that the phone had not answered: whether fairness meant everyone paying or everyone choosing, and whether those could both be fair at once. I held both ideas the way you hold two hot pans, unwilling to set either down.

That night, after close, I stayed to help Romeo haul the grease trap bin to the curb, mostly because I wanted to keep talking to him and could not say so directly. He told me what his dues bought, in dollars per paycheck, and what the last contract had won, and then went quiet, which was unlike him. Behind us the kitchen exhaust fan ticked as it cooled, and the alley smelled of bleach and fryer oil, and the great dramatic question of labor law shrank to two tired guys and a bin of grease, which was its own kind of bathos, though I did not know the word yet. I told him I hadn't decided what I thought about any of it. "Good," Romeo said, and hoisted the bin up over the curb. "Deciding too fast is how Dax got where he is."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: In October 2024 the Los Angeles Times did not endorse a presidential candidate after its owner blocked the editorial board's plans, and several board members resigned in protest.
story:
The note from the principal's office arrived during third period, folded once, and by lunch Natalie had it out on the desk in the newspaper office, smoothing the crease with her palm. Roger read it over her shoulder, and Wyatt leaned back in his chair until its front legs tapped the wall.

"They want the parking lot piece pulled," Roger said. "Or softened."

"'Reviewed for balance,' it says." Wyatt made air quotes with one hand. "Balance. Mr. Ivanova signed it."

The piece in question ran four hundred words: the school had repaved the lot behind the gym, where the asphalt had been crumbling since Natalie's freshman year, while the leaky roof over the arts wing had been patched with tarps for two winters running. A janitor had told her, on the record, that the tarps were the same tarps. The lot, it turned out, sat where a board member's construction company had wanted a showcase project, a detail Natalie had confirmed in the minutes of a meeting nobody attended.

Mr. Ivanova, the faculty adviser, was grading essays in the corner. Natalie carried the note over and set it beside his red pen.

"The principal called me this morning," he said, not looking up. "He thinks the story aggrandize the paper's role at the expense of the school's. His word. He wants you to consider whether it's fair."

"It's documented. Every line."

"I know." He capped the pen. "I told him I'd pass along the concern. That's my job. What you print is yours."

Wyatt snorted from across the room. "That's a dialectic for you. adviser says it's ours, principal says it's his."

But Natalie had stopped listening, because she'd remembered something from October. She pulled her phone from her pocket and searched, and there it was: the Los Angeles Times, that same month, had planned to endorse a presidential candidate, and the paper's owner had blocked the editorial board's plans. No endorsement ran. Several members of the board resigned in protest. She read it twice, then set the phone face-down.

"What," Roger said.

"Nothing. A thing I read."

"Nat."

"In October the LA Times didn't endorse anyone. The owner blocked it. The editorial board wanted to, and the owner said no, and some of them quit over it." She kept her voice flat, the way she did when a fact was still settling into place. "Their paper. Their editorials. And one guy's money decided."

Wyatt spun his chair around. "So what, we quit? We're not exactly the LA Times."

"No." Natalie sat on the edge of the desk, the note still creased in her fingers. "But it's the same question. Who owns the thing decides what the thing says. Our paper isn't owned by anyone, except that it's printed on the school's machines in the school's building with a faculty adviser the school hired." She looked at Mr. Ivanova, who had stopped grading. "That's the part I didn't want to think about."

"I don't tell you what to print," Ivanova said.

"You don't. But you could be made to." She unfolded the note again, read the principal's careful sentences. "I keep wanting this to be simple. He's wrong, we're right, print it. And maybe it's not gratuitous, maybe the connection to the board member is exactly the story. Or maybe I found the connection because I went looking for a villain."

"That's called journalism," Roger said.

"It's called bias until you're sure. I'm not sure." She looked at the clock above the door; the deadline for the printer was four o'clock, ninety minutes away. "Okay. Here's what I think. We run the piece, the whole piece, the tarps and the lot and the minutes. And we run, next to it, a short box saying the principal's office raised concerns about fairness before publication, and that we printed it anyway. Not to spite him. So the reader knows what pressure looks like when it shows up."

"Naming the principal," Wyatt said. "He'll hate that."

"He can write a letter to the editor." Natalie pulled the keyboard toward her and opened the layout file. The parking lot story sat in the second slot, headline already set. She copied the headline into the first slot and started typing the box, three lines, no adjectives. Roger dragged a chair up beside her. Outside, someone was chalking lines on the repaved lot for the spring parking assignments, bright yellow against fresh black, and she watched it a moment through the window before she hit print.

"Gonna be a fun faculty meeting," Wyatt said.

"Probably." Natalie read the box once more on screen. "Print it."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
The cows had to be milked before six, which meant Keira was in the barn with her textbook balanced on a bale, chewing the same paragraph about RNA polymerase for the fourth time, when her cousin wandered in with a jar of tadpoles. Keira had come to the farm for two weeks of her summer before senior year, half for the money her uncle paid her and half because her mother said she needed to be somewhere without a phone signal. The phone signal, as it turned out, reached the barn just fine.

"Are you studying?" her cousin asked, setting the jar on the bale next to the book. She was eleven and treated every question as an accusation.

"Trying to." Keira angled the page away from the splash zone. "Biology. There's a test I have to pass if I want to take the advanced course in the fall."

"Why don't you just know it already?"

"Because it's complicated. Because I keep losing the thread." That was the honest version. The version she'd given Anastasia back in June, over iced coffee, was that she didn't see the point of memorizing what happened inside a cell when she couldn't see inside a cell. Anastasia had said, "You don't have to see it to believe it," and Keira had said, "That's faith, not science," and they'd laughed, but she'd gone on not knowing it.

Her cousin leaned over the jar. One tadpole hung near the glass, gills working. "They're going to be frogs," she said. "How do they know how?"

"Instructions," Keira said. "Everything alive carries instructions. There's a thing called DNA, and it's like the master copy of all the instructions. Every cell has it." She heard herself say master copy and stopped, because a question was coming, and she wasn't sure she could answer it.

"Then how do the instructions get out? If it's the master copy."

There it was. Keira looked at the page, at the diagram she'd been circling like a hawk that never descended, and understood, all at once, that she'd been reading it backwards. "You don't send the master copy out," she said slowly. "That would be like tearing a page out of the only book you own. You make a working copy." She traced the arrow with her finger. "There's an enzyme, called RNA polymerase, and it reads one strand of the DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA. That's the working copy. It carries the gene's instructions out of the nucleus to where they get used." She looked up. "The cell protects the original and sends the copy. That's the whole trick."

"Like when Mom photocopies my birth certificate for camp instead of sending the real one."

"Exactly like that." It had taken her three weeks and a girl with a jar of tadpoles to see what the textbook had been saying plainly all along, and Keira felt both pleased and slightly stupid, the way she felt whenever something simple turned out to have been standing behind her the whole time. The tadpole hung in its green water. Her cousin tapped the glass once and the whole jar shivered.

Later, in the field with the fence wire, she tried to tell Nathalie about it, holding the phone up to catch one bar of signal. "I get it now," she said. "Transcription, translation, all of it. I could teach it."

"Then why do you sound weird about it?"

"Because I had to leave to understand it. I sat in that classroom for a year in a morass of vocabulary and diagrams, and none of it meant anything until a kid asked me why tadpoles know how to be frogs." The wire sagged where she hadn't pulled it tight enough, and she had to walk back and fix it, the phone pressed between shoulder and ear. "My uncle asked if I'm coming back next summer. Full time. He'd amortize the cost of the truck that way, he says. He needs an answer by August."

Nathalie was quiet long enough that Keira could hear the line struggling. "And the advanced course is in the fall. You can't do both."

"I can't do both," Keira agreed. She stood in the gap in the fence with her sleeves pushed up, sunburn forming on the backs of her hands where the classroom had never touched them, thinking that the cell had the right idea: keep the master, send out the copy, and trust the instructions to survive the trip. Except she was not a gene, and her life was not built to be read one strand at a time, and she did not know yet which version of herself was the original and which was the copy sent out into the world. She told Nathalie she'd decide by August. Then she bent, hooked the loose wire with her gloved hand, and pulled it taut against the post.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981.
story:
The volunteer orientation lasted four minutes, which Michael decided was either trust or negligence. Ms. Dang handed him a hairnet, a pair of gloves, and a laminated sheet with the sorting rules, then pointed at a wall clock that read 8:47. "Truck at nine. Doors at ten. Whatever isn't shelved when the line starts, the clients see, so make it look like you know what you're doing." Then she was gone, and Michael was standing between Hussain and a mountain of donated cans with no idea what he was doing.

"Thirty minutes," Hussain said, already pulling boxes toward the pallets. "I've done this twice with my mom. Dented cans are fine unless the dent is on a seam. Bulging cans are out. Nobody wants botulism with their peaches." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and Michael envied that. Hussain could joke while working; Michael had to decide first whether joking was permitted.

They sorted. Michael discovered that a food bank is mostly arithmetic: how many cans of chickpeas fit on a shelf, how many boxes a person can carry if the person refuses to admit a limit. Abhijot arrived at 8:58, breathless, claiming a bus delay, and Ms. Dang made him a coffee without comment, which somehow communicated more disapproval than a speech would have.

"Is there a break after this?" Abhijot asked, stacking soup.

"We've been here eleven minutes," Michael said.

"I'm asking for the future. I plan ahead."

At 9:20 Michael was on a stepladder labeling the dry goods shelf when Abhijot, reading a faded poster near the door as though it were a menu, said, "Huh. This says Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981." He turned around. "Nineteen eighty-one. That's it? My parents are older than food banks in this country."

Michael came down one step. "That can't be right. Food banks are like, an institution. Old churches run them."

"That's what the poster says. Edmonton, January sixteenth, 1981."

"So before that, if you were hungry, what, you just were?" Abhijot held up the poster as evidence, as though Michael had accused him of forging it.

Hussain didn't look up from his pallet. "My dad remembers when the one near us opened. People lined up around the block because there was nothing else. Some of them had jobs." The sentence sat there while all three of them kept working, because it was 9:31 and the doors opened in twenty-nine minutes, and there was no time to stand around being changed by information.

But Michael did feel changed, slightly, in the wrists and the shoulders where the cans were. He had come because his university application wanted "community engagement," a phrase so bombastic that it had made the actual work sound beneath it, a box to tick before the real life of lectures and labs began. He had imagined gratitude, frankly. He had imagined someone thanking him, a small ceremony of recompense, and the thought embarrassed him now, sorting somebody's donated green beans with his name on a timesheet. The work was not about him. It was also, according to the clock, not about feelings at all. Ms. Dang swept past with a pricing gun and said, "Rice goes with rice, Michael, not wherever your arm gets tired," and he carried the rice to where rice lived.

At 9:50 the line was already visible through the front window, which felt unfair, like the audience arriving during rehearsal. Ms. Dang moved along the shelves straightening labels. A woman near the door with two kids waited without fidgeting, and Michael caught himself performing his sympathy in his own head, making a little speech at her, and stopped. He didn't know her. He knew the chickpea count.

"Five minutes," Abhijot said. "We made it. We're heroes."

"We stacked cans," Hussain said.

"Ionize the moment, man. Let it glow."

"It's electrify, and even that's not right."

Michael tightened the last bag of rice and looked at the shelves, which were orderly, which were insufficient, which were forty-three years old as an idea in this country and older than that as a need. He couldn't hold both of those in his head at once, the arithmetic and the history, so he held the rice, which was something. Ms. Dang unlocked the front door and the cold came in ahead of the first people. Michael took his place at the shelf, and when the woman with the two kids reached him, he said, "We've got rice or pasta today," and she said, "What do my kids actually eat, do you think?" and he handed her both before he could decide whether that was allowed.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
Nevaeh had told herself she was coming to the beach to relax, which was why she had brought a printed graph of atmospheric carbon dioxide, a highlighter, and a bottle of sunscreen she never opened. The graph showed a line that crawled sideways for the first half of the century and then bent upward like a branch under snow. She spread it on a towel weighted with two shells and a sneaker, and when Isaiah and Harmony came down the sand with slushies, she did not pretend to be surprised.

"You're studying," Harmony said. "At the beach. In August."

"I'm explaining," Nevaeh said. "Out loud. That's the assignment. Explain how greenhouse gases trap heat, and read this graph, to someone who doesn't already know it. I need practice on actual humans." She was not nervous about the placement test, she had told her mother twice, and here on the towel she told the sand the same thing.

Isaiah commandeered the highlighter before she could object and drew a circle around the steep end of the curve, the way a person draws a target on someone else's homework. "I'll be your human," he said. He wanted the same honors slot, had wanted it since spring, though he kept saying he'd applied on a lark, pure happenstance, the way people say it about things they want very much.

"Fine," Nevaeh said. "Greenhouse gases. Sunlight comes through the air, hits the ground, the ground warms up and gives off heat, and the gases keep some of that heat from escaping back out. More gas, more heat kept. That's the whole idea. Now look at the line."

"That's it?" Isaiah said. "That's your whole explanation?"

"It's the correct whole explanation. The graph is the rest. Carbon dioxide in the air, year by year, back to your great-grandmother. It goes up. Faster lately."

Harmony, who had been lying on her stomach with her slushie sweating into the sand, propped herself on her elbows. "My uncle works at the quarry," she said, apropos of nothing, which was how Harmony introduced most topics. "They had some meeting about it. The quarry, the landfill next to it, the gas off it. He says methane's the real problem and everybody's wasting time on carbon dioxide. My cousin says the opposite. They don't speak at Thanksgiving."

Isaiah sat up straighter, because this was the kind of argument he was built for. "Your uncle's right. Cut the methane and you slow warming way faster. Methane's the strong one."

"It's not that simple," Nevaeh said, and then stopped, because she was not sure how it was not that simple, only that Ms. Clarke-Williams, the retired science teacher three doors down who had agreed to quiz her, had said exactly that with her eyebrows, and Nevaeh had nodded as though she'd understood.

"Okay," Isaiah said. "Per molecule, methane traps way more heat than carbon dioxide. Way more. So if you plug the leaks, you get more bang for it."

"But," Harmony said slowly, still on her elbows, watching the waves do their patient work, "my cousin said the methane doesn't stay. He said a methane molecule is only up there about ten years, something like that. A decade, tops, on average. Carbon dioxide just stays and stays."

Nevaeh looked at the graph, at the line she had traced so many times it felt like a scar on the page. She thought about the difference between a guest who breaks things and a guest who never leaves. "So that's both true," she said. "Methane's stronger, molecule for molecule. And it's gone in about a decade, while the carbon dioxide keeps going. Which means cutting methane leaks would matter more in the next few years, and the carbon dioxide is the long problem, the century problem, the thing that's still in the air when we're old." She said it out loud and felt the two arguments click together like the halves of a shell in her pocket. She also felt the edges of what she couldn't yet say: how the two trades should be weighed, who decides, what counts as soon enough. She was honest enough, at least with the waves, to leave those parts open.

"Mm," Isaiah said, which was the sound he made when someone else got there first.

They walked north along the tideline, the graph folded in Nevaeh's back pocket, arguing about whether the quarry meeting had been about the landfill or the blasting, and Harmony said her uncle's scathing review of the county's air permits was framed in his hallway. Near the rocks a woman in a wide hat was collecting samples in small labeled jars, and when she straightened up Nevaeh recognized her.

"Ms. Clarke-Williams," she said. "You collect things?"

The woman held up a jar of gray water. "I've been retired for two years," she said, "and you've been rehearsing on those two for an hour. I could hear you from the point." She capped the jar. "You finally said something true about methane, near the end. Say it again tomorrow, without the towel."

Nevaeh took the graph out of her pocket, and the wind caught it, and she ran three steps into the surf after it.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2016 ProPublica investigation found that the COMPAS risk tool misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants.
story:
The lab still smelled of the custodian's lemon spray when Anna sat down and pulled up the debate brief on her screen. Across the room, Tanisha was already leaning over her keyboard, and at the front, Ms. Sun was writing "SHOULD ALGORITHMS SET BAIL?" on the whiteboard in blue marker that squeaked against the enamel.

"You're opening for the yes side," Ms. Sun said. "Tanisha rebutts. Then we open the floor."

Anna's argument was the one she had written at midnight, the one she half believed: human judges get tired, hold grudges, read faces and misread them; a program applies the same weights to every defendant, every day, without hunger or bias. She had typed efficiency is fairness and then deleted fairness and typed consistency, because fairness was the word she could not stop chewing on.

She stood when her name was called. The fluorescent lights hummed. She laid out the case in ninety seconds, the scoring function, the training data, the removal of mood and whim. "A judge can be having a bad morning," she finished. "The model can't."

Tanisha did not stand so much as pivot. "You're assuming the data is clean."

"It's data," Anna said. "Numbers."

"Numbers about arrests," Tanisha said. "Numbers about policing."

Ms. Sun raised a hand, two inches, and the room went quiet in the way rooms do when a teacher might do anything. "Back it up," she said. "Either of you. What do you actually know about a real system?"

Nobody spoke. Someone's chair wheeled backward an inch. Anna sat down and, under the desk, opened a search tab, her fingers cold on the keys. She typed COMPAS, because that was the word she had seen in an article her mother left open on the kitchen laptop months ago, something about risk scores and prisons.

The ProPublica investigation surfaced first. She read fast, then slower, the way you reread a sentence to see if it still says what it said. A 2016 investigation of the COMPAS risk tool had found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were misclassified as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants. She read it again. The tool was wrong about the future in a specific direction, and the direction had a color.

"Anna," Ms. Sun said. "You've gone quiet."

"ProPublica," Anna said. "2016. They looked at COMPAS, a real tool courts use. Black defendants who didn't reoffend got labeled high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants who didn't reoffend."

"That's one study," said Lilia from the back, who had been arguing the yes side too, arms folded.

"It's the study," Tanisha said. "It's the one that mattered."

Anna looked at her own brief on the screen, efficiency is consistency, and felt the sentence recalcitrant under her gaze, refusing to become true no matter how she held it. She had wanted the machine to be the neutral party because the humans she had watched, on the news, in courtrooms she'd never entered, were not neutral either. Somewhere behind the argument was a quieter want: to believe that if you removed the person, you removed the problem.

"Here's what I don't get," Lilia said. "The computer doesn't know anyone's race. It's just inputs."

"Inputs come from somewhere," Tanisha said.

"So fix the inputs."

"Who fixes them? Who audits them? The same vendor sells the same model to thirty states and calls it proprietary."

Ms. Sun wrote proprietary on the board without comment. Outside, a lawnmower started and stopped and started again, its uneven drone coming through the sealed window.

Anna stood, and this time she was not reading from the brief. "Okay," she said. "I still think there's something in the consistency argument. A judge can't explain why he set bail at ten thousand instead of five. A model at least has weights you could, in principle, inspect." She paused. "But I just found out my own evidence cuts the other way, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. Twice the rate. That's not a rounding error."

"Then you're switching sides?" Lilia said.

"No. I don't know what I am." Anna heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "Maybe the problem isn't the machine or the judge. Maybe it's the belief that either one can see the future. The whole tool claims to predict who's going to reoffend, and nobody can predict that. It's determinism dressed up as math, and we keep buying the costume."

"Time," Ms. Sun said, though the clock showed four minutes left.

Tanisha was watching Anna with her chin on her fist. "You argued against yourself."

"I argued against the me from midnight," Anna said. "She had it easier."

The bell was two minutes out. Ms. Sun capped the marker. "Friday," she said, "you two co-write the closing. Both sides, honest about what you can't resolve."

Students filed toward the door, screens going dark one by one. Anna stayed to copy the citation into her notebook, the pen pressing hard enough to emboss the next page, because some part of her still wanted a version of this where she could expiate the midnight argument, the lazy confidence of it, by writing it down correctly once.

Tanisha waited by the door. "Library at four?"

"I'll be there," Anna said, and shut the laptop, and the reflection of the empty room slid across the dark screen as she lifted it into her bag.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers.
story:
The exhibition hall smelled like solder and burnt coffee, and Charlotte had forty minutes before the judges reached her team's table. The robot worked. The robot had worked all morning. What she did not have was the second half of the presentation, the algorithm demo, because the code she'd written at two in the morning was checking all nine hundred entries in the parts inventory one at a time and taking eleven seconds to do it.

"That's a linear search," Matias said, leaning over her laptop with his badge lanyard swinging against the table edge. "You're reading the whole shelf to find one screw."

"The shelf is sorted," Rhea said. She said it the way she said most things to Matias lately, flat, already tired of the argument they hadn't started yet. "Part numbers go up left to right. Look at it."

Charlotte looked at it. Nine hundred slots, ordered, and her loop plodding through them like someone feeling along a wall in the dark. It had never occurred to her that the order mattered, that sorting was a thing you could spend rather than just admire.

She cut a sandwich in half without thinking about why, and then thought about why, and stopped chewing. If someone told you the marble was in the left half, you would never search the right half. And a sorted list told you that. Every time you checked the middle, the data itself whispered which half to throw away.

"Binary search," Matias said, watching her type. "Halve it, halve it again. You find any part in ten checks instead of nine hundred." He was already reaching for the whiteboard, drawing a shelf and bisecting it with a marker, which was his way of taking ownership of an idea that hadn't been his.

"Who figured that out?" Rhea asked. It was a genuine question, which surprised Charlotte, because Rhea had spent the whole semester pretending that computer science was beneath her interest, a vocational thing, less romantic than the oceanography videos she watched on her phone during study hall. There was a documentary poster above their club's storage closet, a whale shark hung in blue water, and Rhea had once explained the word pelagic to Charlotte with more tenderness than she had ever explained anything about code: the open ocean, far from shore, where the big slow animals roamed.

Matias frowned at the whiteboard. "Turing, probably. Or Ada Lovelace." He said each name like he was betting on it.

The coding club had taped a paper timeline to the wall by the practice field, ALGORITHMS THROUGH HISTORY, and the three of them drifted toward it during the lunch break, Charlotte still holding her half sandwich. Someone had pinned bubble sort at 1956, quicksort at 1961, the Babylonian square root method floating off at the far left edge like driftwood. A kid from another team was arguing with their advisor about whether Euclid counted, his finger jabbing the paper.

Rhea found it first, because Rhea read everything, including the footnotes nobody printed. "Binary search," she said. "Moore School Lectures." She tapped the small caption under the entry. "John Mauchly, 1946. It was a course on electronic computers. Early." She read it twice, moving her lips the second time.

"Mauchly," Matias said, deflating slightly. "Before quicksort, before bubble sort. Before this whole wall, basically."

"An early course on electronic computers," Charlotte repeated, and felt the strange vertigo of it, that the idea so obvious she'd half-derived it over a sandwich had a birthday, a room, a man standing at a lectern in 1946 explaining to engineers how to stop reading the whole shelf. She wondered what Mauchly's audience had felt, whether anyone had objected that it was too simple to name. She wondered whether it had felt like invention or like admitting something everyone already knew.

The judges came at two. Charlotte ran the demo twice: her old code, eleven seconds of the robot's arm sweeping the shelf slot by slot, and then the new version, the arm dropping immediately to the middle, reading one label, then diving to the left, finding the part in under a second. Mr. Tremblay, the judge with the clipboards and the gray henley, asked why the second one worked, and she started to say because it's faster, and stopped, because that was like saying a whale shark is big.

"The data's sorted," she said. "So every check tells me which half the answer can't be in. I throw half away, then half of what's left. The first version can't learn anything from a wrong guess. It just keeps guessing." She heard Rhea's flat voice in her own and almost laughed. "I only wrote it last night, though. I haven't tested it with a part number that's missing entirely. If it's not there, I'm not sure yet what my loop does. It might spin forever."

Mr. Tremblay wrote something down, and his face gave away nothing about which it was, approval or concern, and beside the table the robot sat with its arm folded over the sorted shelf like a gull waiting at low tide.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post.
story:
Hannah had prepared both sides of the case, which is what she told everyone, and the telling was almost the same as doing it. Almost. The community centre had converted its bingo hall into a courtroom for the evening, folding tables pushed into a U, a hand-lettered sign reading SUPREME COURT OF ROOM 3B, and Ms. Islam presiding from behind a music stand draped in a tablecloth she'd probably brought from home.

The case was a real one, Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., assigned by Ms. Islam two weeks ago with the instruction that each student argue one side and then, without pausing, cross the room and argue the other. Hannah drew the school district first, which felt like being handed the black hat in a western. She'd read the opinion at her kitchen table on Sunday, or most of it, or the parts that surfaced through her phone's glow. What she retained: the Supreme Court had ruled 8 to 1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. That much had stuck, the way a splinter sticks, because of what Karma had said on Saturday night.

Karma had said, "You should delete that before Monday," and Hannah had said, "It's fine, it's my private account," and neither of them had known at the time that the entire Supreme Court had essentially spent a year adjudicating their argument. The post itself was nothing catastrophic, a photo of the losing softball score with a caption about the coach's sagacious decision to bench her in the sixth inning, and the word sagacious had seemed, at 11 p.m., like a reasonable term for a woman who substituted her weakest hitter into a tied game. By Sunday morning it had seemed less reasonable. By Sunday afternoon Hannah was searching the coach's name plus the word "punish" and finding cases, and finding, specifically, this one.

"Petitioner," said Ms. Islam, and Hannah stood up, binder open to a page she had formatted beautifully and read none of.

"Your honors, schools must be able to respond when a student's speech disrupts the team, even if that speech happens off campus." She heard herself say it and, simultaneously, heard Karma saying you should delete that, and understood that she was now arguing for the deletion she had refused. "The post targeted the coach publicly. Discipline was proportionate." Somewhere in the second row, Marion was filming for the class channel, and Hannah thought about how the camera, unlike the Court, had no majority opinion.

Then she crossed the room, as instructed, and stood at the other table, and this part she did not need the binder for. "The Supreme Court ruled 8 to 1," she said, "that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. A post on the weekend, on a private account, is not the school's to police. If it were, every school would be a small jurisdiction with no border, and none of us could say anything, anywhere, that some administrator couldn't reach." Her voice did the thing it did when she actually meant something, and Ms. Islam looked up from her notes.

The two arguments sat in the room together afterward, and Hannah could not cauterize the gap between them the way she'd hoped; both still seemed true to her, or true enough, and the honest position was something like: the student shouldn't have posted it, and the school still shouldn't have punished it, and she could not make those into one clean sentence. When Ms. Islam asked which side she actually believed, Hannah said, "Both, in different lights," which was either wisdom or a dodge, and Ms. Islam's expression declined to adjudicate.

The twist, as Hannah later understood it, was that Karma had reported the post herself. Not to the school, but to Ms. Islam, back when the case was being assigned, and the whole evening had been arranged around Hannah's weekend without anyone saying so. Ms. Islam mentioned it afterward, mildly, while stacking chairs: "Karma thought you'd want to know the law before you found out the hard way."

On the walk home, Hannah deleted the post. Then she undeleted it, screenshotted it first, and sent the screenshot to Karma with the caption "Exhibit A." Karma replied with a single question mark, and Hannah typed, "For my notes. I'm allowed to keep the evidence, it's in the Constitution, probably." She put the phone in her pocket before the reply came.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
Brandon would tell anyone who asked that he had been calm all evening, and he would be lying, which was normal. He had the good seat, the aisle seat his father had surrendered at the turnstile with the sour face of a man doing penance, and from it he could see the whole pitch, the penalty boxes, the fourth official's board, and, most importantly, Hallie's phone, which she held up whenever a call went against their team.

"Offside," she said, though the linesman's flag had stayed down and the striker was celebrating.

"It was onside. His shoulder was level." Brandon did not actually know where the shoulder had been. He had been watching the ball. But a man with an aisle seat develops authority, and he intended to use it.

Julianna leaned past him with her tray of chips. "Then why are they waiting? Nobody's celebrating anymore. Look." The striker had stopped. The referee stood with his hand pressed to his ear, and eighty thousand people stood with him, waiting for a screen none of them could see. Somewhere above them, in a room of monitors, someone was deciding the game.

"That's the video assistant referee," said the woman on Julianna's other side, the neighbour whose name Brandon had forgotten twice this summer. Ms. Dlamini. She said it the way you'd say "the milkman." "They review goals, penalties, direct red cards." She ate a peanut. "Mistaken identity too."

"Right, obviously," Brandon said, though until that sentence he would have sworn the review system covered everything, handballs, offside, fouls anywhere, maybe even the coin toss. "This is the tournament where they introduced it. Russia, 2018. First World Cup with it." That much he knew cold, because he had watched every match of that tournament at eleven years old on his grandfather's sofa, and his grandfather had shouted at the delays until he loved them, because the delays were right more often than the linesman was. It was the only thing his grandfather had ever admitted being wrong about.

Hallie lowered her phone. "So they can overturn a goal for offside?"

"Goals, penalties, red cards, mistaken identity," Ms. Dlamini said again, patient, and Brandon hated how patient, because it implied he hadn't just said the same thing, which he had, first, almost.

The screens flashed. The replay ran its surgical little line across the pitch, and the line said offside by a boot's width, and the referee's arm chopped the goal down, and the stadium made a sound Brandon felt in his teeth. Julianna threw a chip at his head. He let it bounce off, magnanimous, and turned to collect his winnings, because he and Julianna had shaken on it before kickoff: her fifty against his sixty that the goal would stand.

"Level," she said. "He looked level. That line's a millimetre of nothing."

"The line doesn't lie. My grandfather used to say the delay is the price of being right." He was already spending the sixty in his head, and this was the unreliable part, the part he would edit later when he told the story: he had not shaken on sixty. He had shaken on fifty, and he had decided during the replay that inflation had occurred, silently, and that Julianna would probably not remember, and that he could live with probably.

She held out her palm. "Fifty."

"Fifty," he said, as if he had never thought otherwise, and paid her, and the loss stung more than the goal had. Beside him Ms. Dlamini was watching him, and he had the specific paranoia of a person caught. He tried to suture the moment shut with a joke. "VAR for bets. They could review my handshake for mistaken identity."

Her mouth twitched. "They could review your handshake for a direct red card."

"That's pithy," Julianna said, delighted, and Brandon laughed too loudly, because being laughed with covered a great deal.

The match restarted and immediately produced a tackle so bad that both benches stood up, and the referee reached for his ear again, and this time Brandon was the first one saying "red card review, they can do that," before Ms. Dlamini could open her mouth. She let him have it. He watched the monitor room decide a second time, invisible and final, and he thought about how strange it was that eighty thousand people in one place were all watching a single room they could not see, that the whole phenomenology of a stadium, the roar, the terrible intimacy of it, could be suspended by someone alone with screens. His grandfather would have loved this. His grandfather would also have called him a thief over the sixty he had not stolen, only attempted.

No red card came. A yellow, and the tackle's victim limping, and Hallie shouting something at the fourth official that her mother would have to pretend not to have heard.

"It was never fifty," Julianna said, not looking at him, watching the limping player instead. "It was sixty. I saw you decide it was fifty."

The fourth official raised the board for added time. Brandon looked at the pitch, at the screen, at Ms. Dlamini's peanuts.

"Review it," he said, and held out his hand.
